docs.title: Home
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    X[(DataFrame)] --> DP[DataProcessor<br/>model-aware preprocessing]
    DP --> TM[TuningManager<br/>inference · finetune · peft]
    TM --> M[Model<br/>one of 24 vendored TFMs]
    M --> P[predict · predict_proba<br/>evaluate · uncertainty]
    R[(Registry<br/>envelopes + licences)] -. checked before any download .-> TM
    LB[TabularLeaderboard] -. runs many pipelines .-> TM
    TS[(Long time series frame)] --> TSP[TimeSeriesPipeline<br/>forecast · anomalies · impute · embed]

A tabular foundation model (TFM) is a network pretrained on synthetic tables that predicts a new table's targets in context, with no gradient step. TabTune vendors the model code of every supported checkpoint, so one pip install -e . gives you TabPFN, TabICL, Mitra, Orion, Kumo and the rest without installing their packages, and the same TabularPipeline call drives all of them.

There are two parts:

  1. The tabular pipeline. DataProcessor prepares the frame the way the chosen model expects it, TuningManager runs zero-shot inference, full fine-tuning or LoRA, and the torch-free registry checks class counts, feature counts and weight licences before a checkpoint is downloaded. Around it sit a leaderboard, six ensembling strategies, distillation into GBDT or MLP students, conformal uncertainty, shift-aware evaluation and a causal inference module.
  2. The time series pipeline, added in 0.2.1. Same pattern, eleven vendored forecasters plus every tabular model as a forecaster and five statistical baselines. Forecasting, anomaly detection, imputation and embeddings from one fitted model.

  • 24 tabular models, one call

    TabPFN v2 to v3.5, TabICL, Orion-MSP, Orion-BiX, Mitra, ConTextTab, TabDPT, LimiX, TabFM, xRFM, iLTM, EXAONE, Causilo, TabLDM, Kumo. See Models.

  • Three tuning strategies

    inference (zero-shot), finetune (episodic, SFT or native) and peft (LoRA on the layers that matter). See Tuning Strategies.

  • Checks before downloads

    A capability envelope and a weight licence per checkpoint, queried in milliseconds. license_mode="commercial" refuses research-only weights. See Model Registry.

  • Time series

    Chronos, Chronos-Bolt, Chronos-2, TimesFM 3, Toto 1 and 2, TiRex, TiRex-2, Time-MoE, Timestral and T0, with conformal intervals, covariates and backtesting. See Time Series.

  • Uncertainty you can ship

    Split conformal prediction sets and intervals, temperature recalibration and one report with ECE, coverage and set sizes. See Uncertainty.

  • Compare, combine, compress

    TabularLeaderboard ranks models and strategies, TabularEnsemble combines them, TabDistiller turns a teacher into a LightGBM or MLP student.

docs.title: One API for tabular foundation models
docs.text:
TabTune runs and fine-tunes 24 tabular foundation models and 11 time series foundation models behind one scikit-learn style pipeline: fit, predict, evaluate, save, load. Preprocessing, training loops and licence checks are the library's job, not yours.

Get started View on GitHub

v0.2.2 Python 3.10+ PyTorch 2.7+ 24 tabular models 11 time series models MIT code, per-checkpoint weight licences

docs.title: Installation and first run
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/Lexsi-Labs/TabTune.git
cd TabTune
pip install -r requirements.txt
pip install -e .

from tabtune import TabularPipeline

pipe = TabularPipeline(model_name="TabICL", task_type="classification", tuning_strategy="inference")
pipe.fit(X_train, y_train)
print(pipe.evaluate(X_test, y_test))

Swap "TabICL" for any name in tabtune.registry.list_model_names() and nothing else changes.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
TabTune is two pipelines that share one habit: the library adapts to the model, not the other way round.

  1. TabularPipeline wraps 24 tabular foundation models. You name a model, a task and a tuning strategy; preprocessing, the training loop and the licence check are chosen for you.
  2. TimeSeriesPipeline does the same for eleven time series foundation models, every tabular model as a forecaster, and five statistical baselines.

Every row below links to the guide that explains it and, where one exists, to the script under examples/ that runs it. The scripts need the real checkpoints, so most of them want a GPU or patience.

docs.title: Possible use cases
docs.text: Use case How A strong baseline on a new table in a minute TabularPipeline("TabICL") or TabularPipeline("TabPFN") in inference mode. Beat the baseline with your own data tuning_strategy="peft" with the validated loop; it keeps the pretrained weights if nothing beats them. Pick a model you are allowed to ship license_mode="commercial" plus list_models(commercial_ok=True). Compare twelve models before lunch TabularLeaderboard with cache="disk". Serve without a GPU TabDistiller into LightGBM, then ONNX export. Forecast with honest intervals TimeSeriesPipeline("ChronosBolt").calibrate(windows=4).

docs.title: Honest notes
docs.text:
• PEFT is experimental for TabPFN v2 and ConTextTab. Use finetune there if a LoRA run misbehaves.
  • EXAONE's projections are raw parameters, so its peft run wraps zero adapters and proceeds as a full fine-tune. The registry marks this.
  • Every example script downloads real weights on first use. Nothing in tests/ does; the suite runs on CPU with tiny randomly initialised networks.
  • See Known Issues for the full list.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The default DataProcessor is right most of the time. When it is not, you can replace any step or add your own transformer. The usual reasons:

  • Domain-specific feature engineering
  • Specialized encoding for your data
  • Integration with existing pipelines
  • Research and experimentation
  • Non-standard data types

docs.title: Base class interface
docs.text:
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
import pandas as pd

class BasePreprocessor(ABC):
    """Abstract base for all preprocessors."""

    def __init__(self, **kwargs):
        self.config = kwargs

    @abstractmethod
    def fit(self, X: pd.DataFrame, y: pd.Series = None):
        """Learn preprocessing parameters from data."""
        pass

    @abstractmethod
    def transform(self, X: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """Apply preprocessing to data."""
        pass

    def fit_transform(self, X: pd.DataFrame, y: pd.Series = None):
        """Fit and transform in one call."""
        self.fit(X, y)
        return self.transform(X)

    def get_config(self) -> dict:
        """Return preprocessing configuration."""
        return self.config

docs.title: Simple custom preprocessor
docs.text:
Create a basic preprocessor for specialized transformations:

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from tabtune.preprocessing.base import BasePreprocessor
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

class CustomFeatureEngineeringPreprocessor(BasePreprocessor):
    """Custom preprocessor with feature engineering."""

    def __init__(self, scale_numericals=True, create_interactions=True):
        super().__init__(
            scale_numericals=scale_numericals,
            create_interactions=create_interactions
        )
        self.scaler = StandardScaler()
        self.numerical_cols = None
        self.categorical_cols = None

    def fit(self, X: pd.DataFrame, y: pd.Series = None):
        """Learn column types and scaling."""
        # Identify numerical and categorical columns
        self.numerical_cols = X.select_dtypes(
            include=[np.number]
        ).columns.tolist()
        self.categorical_cols = X.select_dtypes(
            include=['object', 'category']
        ).columns.tolist()

        # Fit scaler on numerical columns
        if self.config['scale_numericals']:
            self.scaler.fit(X[self.numerical_cols])

    def transform(self, X: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """Apply transformations."""
        X_transformed = X.copy()

        # Scale numerical features
        if self.config['scale_numericals']:
            X_transformed[self.numerical_cols] = self.scaler.transform(
                X[self.numerical_cols]
            )

        # Create interaction features
        if self.config['create_interactions']:
            X_transformed = self._create_interactions(X_transformed)

        return X_transformed

    def _create_interactions(self, X: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """Create polynomial interaction features."""
        if len(self.numerical_cols) >= 2:
            # Create pairwise interactions
            for i, col1 in enumerate(self.numerical_cols):
                for col2 in self.numerical_cols[i+1:]:
                    X[f'{col1}_x_{col2}'] = X[col1] * X[col2]

        return X

docs.title: Domain-specific preprocessor (finance example)
docs.text:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from tabtune.preprocessing.base import BasePreprocessor

class FinancialDataPreprocessor(BasePreprocessor):
    """Specialized preprocessor for financial data."""

    def __init__(self, 
                 handle_outliers=True,
                 create_ratios=True,
                 normalize_by_scale=True):
        super().__init__(
            handle_outliers=handle_outliers,
            create_ratios=create_ratios,
            normalize_by_scale=normalize_by_scale
        )
        self.outlier_bounds = {}
        self.scaling_factors = {}

    def fit(self, X: pd.DataFrame, y: pd.Series = None):
        """Learn financial data patterns."""
        # Detect outliers (IQR method)
        if self.config['handle_outliers']:
            for col in X.select_dtypes(include=[np.number]):
                Q1 = X[col].quantile(0.25)
                Q3 = X[col].quantile(0.75)
                IQR = Q3 - Q1
                self.outlier_bounds[col] = {
                    'lower': Q1 - 1.5 * IQR,
                    'upper': Q3 + 1.5 * IQR
                }

        # Learn scaling factors by sector
        if self.config['normalize_by_scale']:
            if 'sector' in X.columns:
                for sector in X['sector'].unique():
                    sector_data = X[X['sector'] == sector]
                    self.scaling_factors[sector] = sector_data.mean()

    def transform(self, X: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """Apply financial transformations."""
        X_transformed = X.copy()

        # Handle outliers with clipping
        if self.config['handle_outliers']:
            for col, bounds in self.outlier_bounds.items():
                X_transformed[col] = X_transformed[col].clip(
                    lower=bounds['lower'],
                    upper=bounds['upper']
                )

        # Create financial ratios
        if self.config['create_ratios']:
            if 'revenue' in X_transformed.columns and 'costs' in X_transformed.columns:
                X_transformed['profit_margin'] = (
                    X_transformed['revenue'] - X_transformed['costs']
                ) / X_transformed['revenue']

        # Normalize by sector
        if self.config['normalize_by_scale']:
            if 'sector' in X_transformed.columns:
                for sector, factors in self.scaling_factors.items():
                    sector_mask = X_transformed['sector'] == sector
                    # Normalize numeric columns by sector mean
                    for col in X_transformed.select_dtypes(include=[np.number]):
                        X_transformed.loc[sector_mask, col] /= factors[col]

        return X_transformed

    model_name='TabICL',

docs.title: Chaining preprocessors
docs.text:
Combine multiple preprocessors:

class ChainedPreprocessor(BasePreprocessor):
    """Sequentially apply multiple preprocessors."""

    def __init__(self, preprocessors: list):
        super().__init__(preprocessors=preprocessors)
        self.preprocessor_chain = preprocessors

    def fit(self, X: pd.DataFrame, y: pd.Series = None):
        """Fit each preprocessor in chain."""
        for preprocessor in self.preprocessor_chain:
            preprocessor.fit(X, y)
            X = preprocessor.transform(X)

    def transform(self, X: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """Apply all preprocessors in sequence."""
        for preprocessor in self.preprocessor_chain:
            X = preprocessor.transform(X)
        return X

# Usage
preprocessors = [
    CustomFeatureEngineeringPreprocessor(create_interactions=True),
    FinancialDataPreprocessor(handle_outliers=True),
    YourSpecializedPreprocessor()
]

chained = ChainedPreprocessor(preprocessors)
X_transformed = chained.fit_transform(X_train, y_train)

docs.title: Polynomial features
docs.text:
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures

class PolynomialPreprocessor(BasePreprocessor):
    """Add polynomial features."""

    def __init__(self, degree=2, include_bias=False):
        super().__init__(degree=degree, include_bias=include_bias)
        self.poly = PolynomialFeatures(
            degree=degree,
            include_bias=include_bias
        )
        self.feature_names = None

    def fit(self, X: pd.DataFrame, y: pd.Series = None):
        """Fit polynomial transformer."""
        numerical = X.select_dtypes(include=[np.number])
        self.poly.fit(numerical)
        self.feature_names = self.poly.get_feature_names_out(
            numerical.columns
        )

    def transform(self, X: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """Transform to polynomial features."""
        numerical = X.select_dtypes(include=[np.number])
        poly_features = self.poly.transform(numerical)

        return pd.DataFrame(
            poly_features,
            columns=self.feature_names,
            index=X.index
        )

docs.title: Statistical features
docs.text:
class StatisticalFeaturePreprocessor(BasePreprocessor):
    """Extract statistical features from groups."""

    def __init__(self, groupby_col=None, agg_functions=None):
        super().__init__(
            groupby_col=groupby_col,
            agg_functions=agg_functions or ['mean', 'std', 'min', 'max']
        )

    def fit(self, X: pd.DataFrame, y: pd.Series = None):
        """No fitting needed for statistical features."""
        pass

    def transform(self, X: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """Create statistical aggregates."""
        X_transformed = X.copy()

        if self.config['groupby_col'] and self.config['groupby_col'] in X:
            groupby_col = self.config['groupby_col']

            # Aggregate statistics
            for col in X.select_dtypes(include=[np.number]):
                for func in self.config['agg_functions']:
                    agg_values = X.groupby(groupby_col)[col].agg(func)
                    X_transformed[f'{col}_{func}_by_{groupby_col}'] = (
                        X[groupby_col].map(agg_values)
                    )

        return X_transformed

docs.title: Text feature extraction
docs.text:
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer

class TextFeaturePreprocessor(BasePreprocessor):
    """Extract features from text columns."""

    def __init__(self, text_columns=None, max_features=100):
        super().__init__(
            text_columns=text_columns,
            max_features=max_features
        )
        self.vectorizers = {}

    def fit(self, X: pd.DataFrame, y: pd.Series = None):
        """Fit TF-IDF vectorizers."""
        text_cols = self.config['text_columns'] or [
            col for col in X.columns
            if X[col].dtype == 'object'
        ]

        for col in text_cols:
            vectorizer = TfidfVectorizer(
                max_features=self.config['max_features'],
                lowercase=True
            )
            vectorizer.fit(X[col].astype(str))
            self.vectorizers[col] = vectorizer

    def transform(self, X: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """Transform text to features."""
        X_transformed = X.copy()

        for col, vectorizer in self.vectorizers.items():
            tfidf_matrix = vectorizer.transform(X[col].astype(str))
            feature_names = vectorizer.get_feature_names_out()

            for i, fname in enumerate(feature_names):
                X_transformed[f'{col}_tfidf_{fname}'] = (
                    tfidf_matrix[:, i].toarray().flatten()
                )

        return X_transformed

docs.title: Use scikit-learn transformers
docs.text:
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, RobustScaler
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

class SklearnPreprocessor(BasePreprocessor):
    """Wrap scikit-learn preprocessing pipeline."""

    def __init__(self, steps=None):
        super().__init__(steps=steps or [])
        self.pipeline = Pipeline(steps or [])

    def fit(self, X: pd.DataFrame, y: pd.Series = None):
        """Fit sklearn pipeline."""
        self.pipeline.fit(X, y)

    def transform(self, X: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """Transform using sklearn pipeline."""
        result = self.pipeline.transform(X)
        return pd.DataFrame(result, index=X.index)

# Usage with sklearn pipeline
sklearn_steps = [
    ('scaler', RobustScaler()),
    ('pca', PCA(n_components=50))
]

preprocessor = SklearnPreprocessor(steps=sklearn_steps)
pipeline = TabularPipeline(
    model_name='TabICL',
    processor_params={
        'custom_preprocessor': preprocessor
    }
)

docs.title: Validation framework
docs.text:
class ValidatingPreprocessor(BasePreprocessor):
    """Preprocessor with validation."""

    def __init__(self, validators=None):
        super().__init__(validators=validators or [])
        self.validators = validators

    def validate(self, X: pd.DataFrame) -> dict:
        """Run validators and return results."""
        results = {}

        for validator in self.validators:
            results[validator.name] = validator(X)

        return results

    def fit(self, X: pd.DataFrame, y: pd.Series = None):
        """Fit with validation."""
        validation_results = self.validate(X)

        for name, passed in validation_results.items():
            if not passed:
                print(f"Validation failed: {name}")

class DataQualityValidator:
    """Validate data quality before preprocessing."""

    def __init__(self, name, check_func):
        self.name = name
        self.check_func = check_func

    def __call__(self, X: pd.DataFrame) -> bool:
        """Run validation check."""
        return self.check_func(X)

# Define checks
no_all_nulls = DataQualityValidator(
    'no_all_nulls',
    lambda X: not X.isnull().all().any()
)

sufficient_samples = DataQualityValidator(
    'sufficient_samples',
    lambda X: len(X) >= 100
)

numeric_columns_exist = DataQualityValidator(
    'numeric_columns',
    lambda X: X.select_dtypes(include=[np.number]).shape[1] > 0
)

docs.title: Caching transformed data
docs.text:
from functools import lru_cache
import hashlib

class CachedPreprocessor(BasePreprocessor):
    """Cache preprocessor outputs."""

    def __init__(self, cache_size=128):
        super().__init__(cache_size=cache_size)
        self.cache = {}
        self.cache_size = cache_size

    def _get_cache_key(self, X: pd.DataFrame) -> str:
        """Generate cache key from data hash."""
        data_hash = hashlib.md5(
            pd.util.hash_pandas_object(X).values
        ).hexdigest()
        return data_hash

    def transform(self, X: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """Transform with caching."""
        cache_key = self._get_cache_key(X)

        if cache_key in self.cache:
            return self.cache[cache_key]

        # Perform transformation
        result = self._transform_impl(X)

        # Cache result if space available
        if len(self.cache) < self.cache_size:
            self.cache[cache_key] = result

        return result

    def _transform_impl(self, X: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """Override this for your transformation."""
        return X

docs.title: Parallel processing
docs.text:
from joblib import Parallel, delayed

class ParallelPreprocessor(BasePreprocessor):
    """Apply preprocessing in parallel."""

    def __init__(self, n_jobs=-1, batch_size=1000):
        super().__init__(n_jobs=n_jobs, batch_size=batch_size)

    def transform(self, X: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """Transform in parallel batches."""
        n_jobs = self.config['n_jobs']
        batch_size = self.config['batch_size']

        # Split into batches
        batches = [
            X.iloc[i:i+batch_size]
            for i in range(0, len(X), batch_size)
        ]

        # Process in parallel
        results = Parallel(n_jobs=n_jobs)(
            delayed(self._transform_batch)(batch)
            for batch in batches
        )

        return pd.concat(results, ignore_index=True)

    def _transform_batch(self, batch: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """Override for batch transformation."""
        return batch

class TestCustomPreprocessor(unittest.TestCase):
    """Test custom preprocessor."""

    def setUp(self):
        """Create test data."""
        self.X = pd.DataFrame({
            'A': [1, 2, 3, 4, 5],
            'B': [10, 20, 30, 40, 50],
            'C': ['x', 'y', 'x', 'y', 'z']
        })
        self.y = pd.Series([0, 1, 0, 1, 0])

    def test_fit_transform(self):
        """Test fit_transform."""
        preprocessor = CustomFeatureEngineeringPreprocessor()
        result = preprocessor.fit_transform(self.X, self.y)

        self.assertEqual(len(result), len(self.X))
        self.assertGreater(result.shape[1], self.X.shape[1])

    def test_transform_consistency(self):
        """Test consistency across calls."""
        preprocessor = CustomFeatureEngineeringPreprocessor()
        preprocessor.fit(self.X, self.y)

        result1 = preprocessor.transform(self.X)
        result2 = preprocessor.transform(self.X)

        pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(result1, result2)

    def test_no_data_leakage(self):
        """Test train/test independence."""
        X_train = self.X.iloc[:3]
        X_test = self.X.iloc[3:]

        preprocessor = CustomFeatureEngineeringPreprocessor()
        preprocessor.fit(X_train)

        result_test = preprocessor.transform(X_test)
        self.assertEqual(len(result_test), len(X_test))

docs.title: Real-world example: complete custom pipeline
docs.text:
class ComprehensivePreprocessor(BasePreprocessor):
    """Complete preprocessing pipeline."""

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.numerical_cols = None
        self.categorical_cols = None
        self.transformers = {}

    def fit(self, X: pd.DataFrame, y: pd.Series = None):
        """Fit all transformers."""
        self.numerical_cols = X.select_dtypes(
            include=[np.number]
        ).columns.tolist()
        self.categorical_cols = X.select_dtypes(
            include=['object', 'category']
        ).columns.tolist()

        # Fit numerical transformer
        from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
        self.transformers['scaler'] = StandardScaler()
        self.transformers['scaler'].fit(X[self.numerical_cols])

        # Fit categorical transformer
        from sklearn.preprocessing import LabelEncoder
        self.transformers['encoders'] = {}
        for col in self.categorical_cols:
            le = LabelEncoder()
            le.fit(X[col].astype(str))
            self.transformers['encoders'][col] = le

    def transform(self, X: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """Apply all transformations."""
        X_transformed = pd.DataFrame(index=X.index)

        # Transform numerical
        scaled = self.transformers['scaler'].transform(
            X[self.numerical_cols]
        )
        X_transformed[self.numerical_cols] = scaled

        # Transform categorical
        for col in self.categorical_cols:
            encoded = self.transformers['encoders'][col].transform(
                X[col].astype(str)
            )
            X_transformed[col] = encoded

        return X_transformed

# Usage
preprocessor = ComprehensivePreprocessor()
preprocessor.fit(X_train, y_train)
X_train_processed = preprocessor.transform(X_train)
X_test_processed = preprocessor.transform(X_test)

pipeline = TabularPipeline(
    model_name='TabICL',
    processor_params={'custom_preprocessor': preprocessor}
)

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Most TabTune runs need no tuning: an in-context model has few knobs and sensible defaults. When you do tune, the knobs that matter are the learning rate, the number of epochs, the LoRA rank and the context size, and this page shows how to search them with grid, random and Bayesian strategies, with Optuna and friends. It covers:

  • Search Strategies: Grid search, random search, Bayesian optimization
  • Hyperparameter Spaces: Ranges and distributions for each model
  • Tuning Tools: Integration with Optuna, scikit-optimize, and hyperopt
  • Best Practices: Efficient tuning workflows and validation strategies

docs.text:
Systematic evaluation of all parameter combinations.

Advantages: - Exhaustive coverage - Parallelize easily - Reproducible

Disadvantages: - Exponential complexity - Wasteful on large spaces - Poor scaling

    'epochs': [3, 5],
    'batch_size': [16, 32]
}

# Grid search
best_score = 0
best_params = None

for params in ParameterGrid(param_grid):
    pipeline = TabularPipeline(
        model_name='TabICL',
        tuning_strategy='finetune',
        tuning_params=params
    )

    pipeline.fit(X_train, y_train)

docs.title: Random search
docs.text:
Random sampling from parameter distributions.

Advantages: - Covers parameter space more uniformly - Scales well to large spaces - Simple parallelization

Disadvantages: - May miss optimal region - Less reproducible

import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import uniform, randint

# Define distributions
param_distributions = {
    'learning_rate': uniform(1e-5, 1e-3),
    'epochs': randint(1, 20),
    'batch_size': randint(8, 128),
    'weight_decay': uniform(0.0, 0.1)
}

# Random search
n_iter = 20
best_score = 0
best_params = None

for i in range(n_iter):
    # Sample random parameters
    params = {
        key: dist.rvs()
        for key, dist in param_distributions.items()
    }

    # Convert to integers
    params['epochs'] = int(params['epochs'])
    params['batch_size'] = int(params['batch_size'])

    pipeline = TabularPipeline(
        model_name='TabICL',
        tuning_strategy='finetune',
        tuning_params=params
    )

    pipeline.fit(X_train, y_train)
    score = pipeline.evaluate(X_val, y_val)['accuracy']

    if score > best_score:
        best_score = score
        best_params = params
        print(f"Iteration {i+1}/{n_iter}: {score:.4f}")

print(f"\nBest parameters: {best_params}")

docs.title: Bayesian optimization with Optuna
docs.text:
Intelligent search using Gaussian processes.

Advantages: - Intelligent sampling - Few evaluations needed - Adaptively explores promising regions

Disadvantages: - More complex - Slower per iteration - Requires more setup

import optuna
from optuna.pruners import MedianPruner

def objective(trial):
    """Optuna objective function."""

    # Suggest hyperparameters
    learning_rate = trial.suggest_float('learning_rate', 1e-5, 1e-3, log=True)
    epochs = trial.suggest_int('epochs', 1, 20)
    batch_size = trial.suggest_int('batch_size', 8, 128)
    weight_decay = trial.suggest_float('weight_decay', 0.0, 0.1)

    tuning_params = {
        'device': 'cuda',
        'learning_rate': learning_rate,
        'epochs': epochs,
        'batch_size': batch_size,
        'weight_decay': weight_decay
    }

    # Train and evaluate
    pipeline = TabularPipeline(
        model_name='TabICL',
        tuning_strategy='finetune',
        tuning_params=tuning_params
    )

    pipeline.fit(X_train, y_train)
    score = pipeline.evaluate(X_val, y_val)['accuracy']

    return score

# Create study
study = optuna.create_study(
    direction='maximize',
    pruner=MedianPruner()
)

# Optimize
study.optimize(objective, n_trials=50, n_jobs=1)

# Get results
print(f"Best score: {study.best_value:.4f}")
print(f"Best parameters: {study.best_params}")

docs.title: k-fold cross-validation
docs.text:
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold
import numpy as np

def cross_validate_hyperparams(X, y, model_name, params, k=5):
    """Evaluate hyperparameters via k-fold CV."""

    kf = KFold(n_splits=k, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
    scores = []

    for fold_idx, (train_idx, val_idx) in enumerate(kf.split(X)):
        X_train_fold = X.iloc[train_idx]
        X_val_fold = X.iloc[val_idx]
        y_train_fold = y.iloc[train_idx]
        y_val_fold = y.iloc[val_idx]

        # Train and evaluate
        pipeline = TabularPipeline(
            model_name=model_name,
            tuning_strategy='finetune',
            tuning_params=params
        )

        pipeline.fit(X_train_fold, y_train_fold)
        score = pipeline.evaluate(X_val_fold, y_val_fold)['accuracy']
        scores.append(score)

        print(f"Fold {fold_idx+1}/{k}: {score:.4f}")

    mean_score = np.mean(scores)
    std_score = np.std(scores)

    print(f"\nMean: {mean_score:.4f} ± {std_score:.4f}")

    return mean_score, std_score

# Usage
mean, std = cross_validate_hyperparams(
    X_train, y_train,
    model_name='TabICL',
    params={'epochs': 5, 'learning_rate': 2e-5},
    k=5
)

docs.title: Early stopping during tuning
docs.text:
class EarlyStoppingTuner:
    """Tuner with early stopping."""

    def __init__(self, patience=3):
        self.patience = patience
        self.best_score = 0
        self.no_improve_count = 0

    def should_stop(self, score):
        """Check if tuning should stop."""
        if score > self.best_score:
            self.best_score = score
            self.no_improve_count = 0
            return False
        else:
            self.no_improve_count += 1
            return self.no_improve_count >= self.patience

# Usage
tuner = EarlyStoppingTuner(patience=5)

for params in param_grid:
    # ... train and evaluate ...

    if tuner.should_stop(score):
        print(f"Early stopping after {tuner.no_improve_count} iterations")
        break

docs.text:
import optuna

def objective_with_pruning(trial):
    """Objective with early pruning."""

    learning_rate = trial.suggest_float('lr', 1e-5, 1e-3, log=True)
    epochs = trial.suggest_int('epochs', 1, 20)

    pipeline = TabularPipeline(
        model_name='TabICL',
        tuning_strategy='finetune',
        tuning_params={
            'learning_rate': learning_rate,
            'epochs': epochs
        }
    )

    # Train with intermediate reporting
    for epoch in range(epochs):
        # ... train for one epoch ...

        # Evaluate
        score = pipeline.evaluate(X_val, y_val)['accuracy']

        # Report intermediate value
        trial.report(score, epoch)

        # Prune if not promising
        if trial.should_prune():
            raise optuna.TrialPruned()

    return score

# Create study with pruning
study = optuna.create_study(
    direction='maximize',
    pruner=optuna.pruners.MedianPruner()
)

study.optimize(objective_with_pruning, n_trials=30)

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Where the memory goes in a TabTune run, and what to do when it runs out. This matters when you are:

  • Training on GPUs with limited VRAM (< 8GB)
  • Processing large datasets (100K+ rows)
  • Using large model architectures
  • Running multiple experiments simultaneously
  • Deploying in resource-constrained environments

Memory Breakdown (typical forward/backward pass):

Model weights:        40-50% (frozen in PEFT)
Optimizer states:     20-30% (momentum, variance)
Gradients:           10-15%
Activations:         10-20% (intermediate values)
DataLoader buffers:   5-10%
─────────────────────────────
Total:               100%

docs.text:
import psutil
import nvidia_smi

class MemoryMonitor:
    """Monitor memory usage during training."""

    def __init__(self):
        self.peak_gpu = 0
        self.peak_cpu = 0

    def record(self):
        """Record current memory usage."""
        try:
            nvidia_smi.nvmlInit()
            handle = nvidia_smi.nvmlDeviceGetHandleByIndex(0)
            info = nvidia_smi.nvmlDeviceGetMemoryInfo(handle)
            gpu_mem = info.used / 1e9

            self.peak_gpu = max(self.peak_gpu, gpu_mem)
        except:
            gpu_mem = 0

        # CPU memory
        process = psutil.Process()
        cpu_mem = process.memory_info().rss / 1e9
        self.peak_cpu = max(self.peak_cpu, cpu_mem)

        return gpu_mem, cpu_mem

    def report(self):
        """Print memory report."""
        print(f"Peak GPU: {self.peak_gpu:.2f} GB")
        print(f"Peak CPU: {self.peak_cpu:.2f} GB")

# Usage
monitor = MemoryMonitor()

# Periodically call during training
for epoch in range(num_epochs):
    gpu_mem, cpu_mem = monitor.record()
    print(f"Epoch {epoch}: GPU {gpu_mem:.2f}GB, CPU {cpu_mem:.2f}GB")

monitor.report()

docs.title: Real-time memory tracking
docs.text:
import logging
from datetime import datetime

class MemoryTracker:
    """Track memory throughout training."""

    def __init__(self, log_interval=100):
        self.log_interval = log_interval
        self.iteration = 0
        self.history = []

    def step(self):
        """Call after each training step."""
        self.iteration += 1

        if self.iteration % self.log_interval == 0:
            peak = torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() / 1e9
            current = torch.cuda.memory_allocated() / 1e9

            self.history.append({
                'iteration': self.iteration,
                'peak': peak,
                'current': current,
                'time': datetime.now()
            })

            print(f"[{self.iteration}] Peak: {peak:.2f}GB, Current: {current:.2f}GB")

    def plot(self):
        """Plot memory over time."""
        import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

        iterations = [h['iteration'] for h in self.history]
        peaks = [h['peak'] for h in self.history]

        plt.plot(iterations, peaks)
        plt.xlabel('Iteration')
        plt.ylabel('Peak Memory (GB)')
        plt.title('GPU Memory Usage Over Time')
        plt.show()

# Usage
tracker = MemoryTracker()

for batch in dataloader:
    # ... training step ...
    tracker.step()

tracker.plot()

def safe_train(model, dataloader, max_retries=3):
    """Train with automatic memory adaptation."""

    batch_size = 32

    for attempt in range(max_retries):
        try:
            # Try training with current batch size
            for batch in dataloader:
                # ... training code ...
                pass

            return  # Success

        except RuntimeError as e:
            if 'out of memory' in str(e).lower():
                # Reduce batch size and retry
                batch_size //= 2
                print(f"OOM detected. Retrying with batch_size={batch_size}")

                # Clear cache
                torch.cuda.empty_cache()

                # Recreate dataloader with smaller batch
                dataloader = DataLoader(
                    dataset,
                    batch_size=batch_size
                )
            else:
                raise

    raise RuntimeError(f"Failed after {max_retries} attempts")

from tabtune import TabularPipeline
import torch

def memory_optimized_training(
    X_train, y_train, X_val, y_val,
    gpu_memory_gb=4
):
    """Train with automatic memory optimization."""

    # Determine configuration
    if gpu_memory_gb < 4:
        use_peft = True
        batch_size = 4
        support_size = 32
        mixed_precision = 'fp16'
        rank = 2
    elif gpu_memory_gb < 8:
        use_peft = True
        batch_size = 8
        support_size = 64
        mixed_precision = 'fp16'
        rank = 4
    else:
        use_peft = False
        batch_size = 32
        support_size = 128
        mixed_precision = None
        rank = 8

    # Create pipeline
    strategy = 'peft' if use_peft else 'finetune'

    tuning_params = {
        'device': 'cuda',
        'epochs': 5,
        'learning_rate': 2e-4 if use_peft else 2e-5,
        'batch_size': batch_size,
        'support_size': support_size,
        'num_workers': 0,
        'pin_memory': False if gpu_memory_gb < 4 else True
    }

    if mixed_precision:
        tuning_params['mixed_precision'] = mixed_precision

    if use_peft:
        tuning_params['peft_config'] = {
            'r': rank,
            'lora_alpha': 2 * rank,
            'lora_dropout': 0.05
        }

    pipeline = TabularPipeline(
        model_name='TabICL',
        tuning_strategy=strategy,
        tuning_params=tuning_params
    )

    # Train with monitoring
    print(f"Training with strategy={strategy}, batch_size={batch_size}")
    pipeline.fit(X_train, y_train)

    # Evaluate
    metrics = pipeline.evaluate(X_val, y_val)
    print(f"Validation accuracy: {metrics['accuracy']:.4f}")

    return pipeline

# Usage
pipeline = memory_optimized_training(
    X_train, y_train, X_val, y_val,
    gpu_memory_gb=4
)

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
TabTune's training loops are single-process. Spreading a run over several GPUs is still possible, in three ways:

  • Data Parallelism: Distribute data across GPUs
  • Model Parallelism: Distribute model across GPUs
  • Distributed Optimization: Synchronized gradient updates
  • Scaling: Near-linear speedup with multiple GPUs

docs.title: Parallelism strategies
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Multi-GPU Training] --> B[Data Parallelism]
    A --> C[Model Parallelism]
    A --> D[Pipeline Parallelism]

    B --> B1["Each GPU gets data batch"]
    B --> B2["Model replicated on each GPU"]
    B --> B3["Gradients averaged across GPUs"]

    C --> C1["Model layers split across GPUs"]
    C --> C2["Each GPU processes different layers"]
    C --> C3["Communication between GPUs"]

    D --> D1["Stages of model pipeline"]
    D --> D2["Different stages on different GPUs"]
    D --> D3["Micro-batching for efficiency"]

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class DataParallelWrapper:
    """Wrap TabTune pipeline with DataParallel."""

    def __init__(self, model, device_ids=None):
        self.model = nn.DataParallel(model, device_ids=device_ids)

        """Training with DataParallel."""
        # Batch automatically split across GPUs
        return self.model.module.fit(X_train, y_train, **kwargs)

    def predict(self, X_test):
        """Inference on primary GPU."""
        return self.model.module.predict(X_test)

# Usage

import os
import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
from torch.nn.parallel import DistributedDataParallel
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, DistributedSampler
from tabtune import TabularPipeline

def main():
    """Main training function."""

    # Initialize distributed training
    dist.init_process_group(backend='nccl')
    rank = dist.get_rank()
    world_size = dist.get_world_size()

    # Set device
    device = torch.device(f'cuda:{rank}')
    torch.cuda.set_device(device)

    # Print rank info
    if rank == 0:
        print(f"Training on {world_size} GPUs")

    # Load data
    X_train, y_train = load_data()

    # Create distributed sampler
    train_sampler = DistributedSampler(
        dataset=range(len(X_train)),
        num_replicas=world_size,
        rank=rank,
        shuffle=True
    )

    # Create dataloader
    train_loader = DataLoader(
        train_sampler,
        batch_size=32,
        num_workers=2
    )

    # Create model
    pipeline = TabularPipeline(
        model_name='TabICL',
        tuning_strategy='finetune',
        tuning_params={
            'device': device,
            'epochs': 5,
            'learning_rate': 2e-5
        }
    )

    # Wrap with DistributedDataParallel
    pipeline.model = DistributedDataParallel(
        pipeline.model,
        device_ids=[rank]
    )

    # Training
    if rank == 0:
        print("Starting training...")

    pipeline.fit(X_train[train_sampler.indices], y_train[train_sampler.indices])

    # Evaluation on rank 0 only
    if rank == 0:
        metrics = pipeline.evaluate(X_test, y_test)
        print(f"Validation Accuracy: {metrics['accuracy']:.4f}")

    # Cleanup
    dist.destroy_process_group()

if __name__ == '__main__':

def train_with_sync():
    """Training with synchronization points."""

    dist.init_process_group(backend='nccl')
    rank = dist.get_rank()

    # Training
    for epoch in range(num_epochs):
        # ... training code ...

        # Synchronize all ranks
        dist.barrier()

        # Evaluation (on rank 0 only)
        if rank == 0:
            metrics = evaluate()
            print(f"Epoch {epoch}: {metrics}")

        # Broadcast best checkpoint from rank 0
        if rank == 0:
            best_state = pipeline.model.state_dict()
        else:
            best_state = None

        # Distribute to all ranks
        dist.broadcast_object_list([best_state], src=0)

        if rank != 0:
            pipeline.model.load_state_dict(best_state[0])

    dist.destroy_process_group()

def train_with_accumulation(num_accumulation_steps=4):
    """Training with gradient accumulation."""

    optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters())

    for epoch in range(num_epochs):
        for i, batch in enumerate(dataloader):
            # Forward pass
            loss = model(batch)

            # Backward (accumulate gradients)
            (loss / num_accumulation_steps).backward()

            # Update weights
            if (i + 1) % num_accumulation_steps == 0:
                optimizer.step()
                optimizer.zero_grad()

from torch.cuda.amp import autocast, GradScaler

def train_mixed_precision():
    """Multi-GPU training with mixed precision."""

    scaler = GradScaler()

    for epoch in range(num_epochs):
        for batch in dataloader:
            # Forward with autocast
            with autocast(dtype=torch.float16):
                loss = model(batch)

            # Backward with scaling
            scaler.scale(loss).backward()

            # All-reduce scaled gradients
            for param in model.parameters():
                if param.grad is not None:
                    dist.all_reduce(param.grad)

            # Update weights
            scaler.step(optimizer)
            scaler.update()

docs.title: Load imbalance
docs.text:
# Problem: Some GPUs finish before others
# Solution: Dynamic load balancing

def balanced_sampler(dataset, num_replicas, rank):
    """Create balanced sampler across ranks."""

    # Ensure each rank gets similar amount of work
    samples_per_rank = len(dataset) // num_replicas
    remainder = len(dataset) % num_replicas

    start = rank * samples_per_rank + min(rank, remainder)
    end = start + samples_per_rank + (1 if rank < remainder else 0)

    indices = list(range(start, end))
    return DistributedSampler(
        indices,
        num_replicas=num_replicas,
        rank=rank
    )

# Problem: Different GPUs compute different gradients
# Solution: Proper synchronization

def synchronized_training():
    """Ensure all ranks have synchronized gradients."""

    for batch in dataloader:
        # Compute gradients
        loss = model(batch)
        loss.backward()

        # Synchronize gradients across all ranks
        for param in model.parameters():
            dist.all_reduce(param.grad)
            param.grad /= world_size  # Average

        # Update
        optimizer.step()

    device = torch.device(f'cuda:{rank}')

    if rank == 0:
        print(f"Starting training on {world_size} GPUs")

    # Load data
    X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test = load_dataset()

    # Scale learning rate with batch size
    scaled_lr = args.learning_rate * world_size

    # Create pipeline
    pipeline = TabularPipeline(
        model_name='TabICL',
        tuning_strategy='finetune',
        tuning_params={
            'device': device,
            'epochs': args.epochs,
            'learning_rate': scaled_lr,
            'batch_size': args.batch_size
        }
    )

    # Wrap with DDP
    pipeline.model = DistributedDataParallel(
        pipeline.model,
        device_ids=[rank]
    )

    # Training
    if rank == 0:
        print(f"Training with LR={scaled_lr:.2e}, batch_size={args.batch_size}")

    pipeline.fit(X_train, y_train)

    # Synchronize before evaluation
    dist.barrier()

    # Evaluation on primary GPU only
    if rank == 0:
        metrics = pipeline.evaluate(X_test, y_test)
        print(f"Final accuracy: {metrics['accuracy']:.4f}")

    dist.destroy_process_group()

if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

Launch: 

torchrun --nproc_per_node=4 train_distributed.py --epochs 5 --batch_size 32

docs.title: What is PEFT?
docs.text:
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) adapts a pretrained model by training a small fraction of its parameters. Compared with a full fine-tune it cuts:

  • Memory consumption (90% reduction)
  • Training time (2-3x speedup)
  • Storage requirements (only store small adapters)

docs.title: What is LoRA?
docs.text:
Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is a specific PEFT technique that:

  • Freezes pre-trained model weights
  • Adds small trainable "adapter" layers
  • Uses low-rank decomposition for efficiency
  • Trains only 1-10% of parameters

docs.title: What is new
docs.text:
Instead of updating all weights, LoRA learns a low-rank approximation of weight updates:

\[ W' = W_0 + \Delta W = W_0 + BA \]

Where: - \(W_0\): Original frozen weights (large) - \(\Delta W = BA\): Low-rank decomposition - \(A\): Input projection (small) - \(B\): Output projection (small) - \(r\): Rank (typically 4-16, much smaller than weight dimensions)

docs.title: Low-rank decomposition
docs.text:
For a weight matrix \(W \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{out} \times d_{in}}\), LoRA represents updates as:

\[ \Delta W = BA, \quad B \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{out} \times r}, A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times d_{in}} \]

Complexity Reduction: - Full weights: \(d_{out} \times d_{in}\) parameters - LoRA: \(r(d_{out} + d_{in})\) parameters - Compression ratio: \(\frac{r(d_{out} + d_{in})}{d_{out} \times d_{in}}\)

Example: For a 768×768 weight matrix: - Full: 589,824 parameters - LoRA (r=8): 12,288 parameters - Compression: 98% reduction

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text:
To balance adaptation magnitude, LoRA scales the output:

\[ h = W_0 x + \alpha \frac{1}{r} B(Ax) \]

Where \(\alpha\) (lora_alpha) controls the scaling factor \(\frac{\alpha}{r}\).

Effect of Alpha: - Higher alpha: Larger adaptation magnitude - Default: \(\alpha = 2r\) (empirically optimal)

docs.title: Dropout
docs.text:
Dropout is applied to the input before LoRA projection for regularization:

\[ h = W_0 x + \alpha \frac{1}{r} B(\text{dropout}(Ax)) \]

docs.title: LoRA configuration
docs.text:
peft_config = {
    'r': 8,                    # Rank (main hyperparameter)
    'lora_alpha': 16,          # Scaling factor
    'lora_dropout': 0.05,      # Dropout probability
    'target_modules': None,    # Modules to adapt (model default)
    'bias': 'none'             # Bias handling
}

docs.title: LoRA linear layer
docs.text:
TabTune implements LoRALinear that wraps standard PyTorch linear layers:

class LoRALinear(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, base_linear, r=8, alpha=16, dropout=0.05):
        super().__init__()
        self.base = base_linear          # Frozen base layer
        self.lora_A = nn.Linear(..., r)  # Adapter A
        self.lora_B = nn.Linear(r, ...)  # Adapter B
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout)
        self.scaling = alpha / r

    def forward(self, x):
        # Base forward (no gradients)
        base_out = self.base(x)
        # LoRA forward
        lora_out = self.lora_B(self.lora_A(self.dropout(x))) * self.scaling
        return base_out + lora_out

docs.title: Weight freezing
docs.text:
• Base model weights: requires_grad=False
  • LoRA adapters: requires_grad=True
  • Enables gradient computation only on adapters

docs.title: Rank selection
docs.text:
The rank r is the most critical hyperparameter:

Rank Parameters Memory Accuracy Speed r=2 Minimal Very Low Lower r=4 Low Low Good r=8 Moderate Moderate Better r=16 High High Best r=32 Very High Very High Optimal

Guidelines: - Small data (10K): r=4 (enough for adaptation) - Medium data (100K): r=8 (balanced) - Large data (1M): r=16 (more expressive) - Very constrained: r=2 (minimum viable)

Rule of Thumb: [ r = \max(4, \frac{\text{dataset_size}}{50000}) ]

docs.title: Alpha selection
docs.text:
Alpha controls the magnitude of LoRA contribution:

# Recommended: alpha = 2 * rank
peft_config = {
    'r': 8,
    'lora_alpha': 16,  # = 2 * 8
    'lora_dropout': 0.05
}

Effects: - Alpha too low: Adaptation weak, training slow - Alpha = 2r: Empirically optimal - Alpha too high: Training unstable, may diverge

docs.title: Dropout probability
docs.text:
LoRA dropout acts as regularization:

lora_dropout_values = {
    0.0: 'No regularization (may overfit)',
    0.05: 'Light regularization (default)',
    0.1: 'Moderate regularization',
    0.2: 'Strong regularization (for small data)'
}

Selection: - Large data: 0.05 (default) - Small data: 0.1-0.2 (prevent overfitting) - Already regularized model: 0.0-0.05

docs.title: Module hierarchy
docs.text:
TabTune identifies target modules via pattern matching:

# LoRA targets linear transformation layers
target_modules = {
    'column_embeddings': 'Column feature processing',
    'row_attention': 'Row-wise interactions',
    'prediction_head': 'Final prediction',
    'decoder': 'Feature reconstruction'
}

docs.title: Model-specific defaults
docs.text:
Each model has pre-configured target modules optimized for LoRA:

TabICL: 

target_modules = [
    'col_embedder.tf_col',
    'row_interactor',
    'icl_predictor.tf_icl',
    'icl_predictor.decoder'
]

TabDPT: 

target_modules = [
    'transformer_encoder',
    'encoder',
    'y_encoder',
    'head'
]

Mitra: 

target_modules = [
    'x_embedding',
    'layers',
    'final_layer'
]

docs.title: Custom target selection
docs.text:
Override defaults for specific needs:

pipeline = TabularPipeline(
    model_name='TabICL',
    tuning_strategy='peft',
    tuning_params={
        'peft_config': {
            'r': 8,
            'lora_alpha': 16,
            'target_modules': [
                'col_embedder.tf_col',  # Only column embedder
                'icl_predictor.decoder'   # Plus decoder
            ]
        }
    }
)

docs.title: Typical training loop
docs.text:
from tabtune import TabularPipeline

# Create pipeline with PEFT
pipeline = TabularPipeline(
    model_name='TabICL',
    tuning_strategy='peft',
    tuning_params={
        'device': 'cuda',
        'epochs': 5,
        'learning_rate': 2e-4,  # Typically higher than finetune
        'peft_config': {'r': 8, 'lora_alpha': 16}
    }
)

# Training (only adapters are updated)
pipeline.fit(X_train, y_train)

# Inference
predictions = pipeline.predict(X_test)

docs.title: Learning rate strategy
docs.text:
LoRA uses different learning rates than base fine-tuning:

# Base fine-tuning (all parameters)
learning_rate_base_ft = 2e-5

# LoRA fine-tuning (small parameters)
learning_rate_peft = 2e-4  # 10x higher typical

# Rationale: Smaller parameter updates need larger learning rates

docs.title: Optimizer configuration
docs.text:
# LoRA-specific optimizer settings
optimizer_config = {
    'optimizer': 'adamw',
    'learning_rate': 2e-4,
    'weight_decay': 0.01,
    'eps': 1e-8,
    'betas': (0.9, 0.999)
}

# Explore memory-speed-accuracy trade-off
configs = [
    {'r': 2, 'name': 'Ultra-Light'},

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: All notable changes to TabTune. The format follows Keep a Changelog.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• LimiX-2 (LimiXv2): Stable AI's 400M-parameter LimiX-2, vendored from LimiX inference/v2_0 and model/v2_0. Classification, regression, episodic fine-tuning and LoRA. LimiX v1 stays Limix.
  • NVIDIA Kumo Tabular (KumoTabular): small, medium and large checkpoints of NVIDIA structured-data-models. Classification, regression, episodic fine-tuning and LoRA.
  • TabAbax (TabAbax): BaiRong's TabICLv2-derived model, vendored from the TabAbax source tree. Classification, regression, episodic fine-tuning and LoRA through the model's own training branch.
  • Timestral (Timestral): Mistral AI's Decoupled Horizon Forecasting models, 5M to 209M. Multivariate targets, past, known and categorical covariates, 21 quantiles, fine-tuning and LoRA, on TimeSeriesPipeline.
  • T0 (T0): The Forecasting Company's t0-alpha, -beta and -gamma. Multivariate targets, known covariates, any quantile level, fine-tuning and LoRA.
  • A validated episodic fine-tuning driver (tabtune.TuningManager.episodic_finetune) used by Kumo, LimiX-2 and TabAbax: held-out validation scored through the real inference path, the pretrained weights as the epoch-0 baseline, warmup and cosine schedule, stratified support sets sized like the inference context, gradient accumulation, early stopping, best weights restored (pretrained weights as the fallback), and a finetune_report_ on the estimator. Replaces the fixed-schedule loops under which every fine-tuned run scored worse than zero-shot on the models' own benchmark.
  • pyarrow as a core dependency (Kumo's tensor backend), and typeguard>=2.13.3,<3, which the vendored TabFM estimator imports through jaxtyping.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text: • A regression pipeline without an explicit finetune_mode uses meta-learning for models that register no turn_by_turn mode (Kumo, LimiX-2, TabAbax, Causilo, TabLDM) instead of warning.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Time series on TimeSeriesPipeline. The same pipeline pattern as tabular: TimeSeriesPipeline(model_name, task_type, tuning_strategy, tuning_params, model_params, forecast_params) with fit, predict, evaluate, save and load. Tasks are forecasting, anomaly detection, imputation and embeddings; strategies are zero-shot inference, finetune and peft. Conformal calibrate(), rolling-origin backtest(), context-length tuning and select(), plus TimeSeriesLeaderboard, TimeSeriesEnsemble and TimeSeriesBenchmark.
  • Nine vendored time series foundation models: Chronos, Chronos-Bolt, Chronos-2, TimesFM 3, Toto 1, Toto 2, TiRex, TiRex-2, Time-MoE.
  • Five new tabular models: TabPFN v3.5 and v3.5-fast (Prior Labs), Causilo (Nums AI), TabLDM (Xiaomi) and Mitra v2 (AWS), in the registry with envelopes and weight licences. Their preprocessing needs skrub, now a core dependency.
  • Tabular models as forecasters: TabPFN-TS on the vendored TabPFN, TabularTS-<name> for every tabular model with a regression head, and the weight-free TabularTS-GBM.
  • tabtune.bridge.SeriesFeaturizer: leak-safe features of an entity's history for any tabular model.
  • The tabtune timeseries command line group.
  • One logger: setup_logger configures Rich, plain or JSON output and rotating files once.

docs.title: Removed
docs.text: • The tabtune.tsfm facade.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Seven models: EXAONE Tabular, xRFM, iLTM, TabFM, TabPFN v3, TabICL v2, TabPFN v2.6.
  • A torch-free model registry: ModelSpec per checkpoint with a capability envelope and a weight licence, list_models, get_model_spec, check_envelope, check_license, register_model, and the exception hierarchy (TabTuneError, ConfigError, ModelNotFoundError, UnsupportedTaskError, UnsupportedStrategyError, EnvelopeError, LicenseError). New TabularPipeline keyword-only parameters envelope_mode, license_mode, validate.
  • Uncertainty: ConformalClassifier (lac, aps), ConformalRegressor (absolute, cqr), Recalibrator, uncertainty_report() with ECE, MCE, Brier, coverage, set sizes and size-stratified coverage. A calibration frame that overlaps training is detected by fingerprint and raises.
  • Shift-aware evaluation: TemporalSplit (with embargo gap), GroupedSplit, StratifiedGroupedSplit, ShiftEvaluator reporting the IID-to-shift gap. Shared metrics in tabtune.evaluation.metrics.
  • Typed configuration: PipelineConfig, TuningConfig, PeftConfig, ProcessorConfig, ContextSamplingConfig, YAML round trips, validate_against_registry(). Unknown keys in plain dicts now warn instead of vanishing.
  • Prediction caching: cache="memory" or "disk".
  • Causal inference: CausalAnalysis with DML, S/T/X/R-learners and causal forests, identification, refutation, proxy auditing and counterfactual fairness.
  • Distillation: TabDistiller into LightGBM, XGBoost, CatBoost or MLP students, single and multi-teacher, ONNX export.
  • Lazy imports: import tabtune no longer pulls in torch or transformers.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• OrionMSP v1.5 and LimiX.
  • The regression framework: unified training, standard metrics, benchmark structure.
  • The resampling module: context-aware support/query sampling and episodic batching.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• base-ft renamed finetune.
  • Better memory management, gradient stability for the MSP models, Colab compatibility, wider serialisation.
• First release: TabularPipeline, DataProcessor, TuningManager, TabularLeaderboard, nine models, the first documentation site.

docs.title: Contributing to TabTune
docs.text: Thanks for considering it. Bug reports, model integrations, documentation fixes and benchmark results are all useful. This page is the whole process.

docs.title: Set up
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/<you>/TabTune.git
cd TabTune
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
pip install -e ".[dev,docs]"
pre-commit install

Run the suite before you start, so you know what green looks like on your machine:

pytest -q                 # about 1,600 tests, CPU only, no downloads
pytest tests/test_registry.py tests/test_imports.py   # the fast ones

Nothing in tests/ downloads weights. Tests that need a real checkpoint are marked and skip when it is absent.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
• ruff, black and isort run through pre-commit; the CI runs them too.
  • Type hints on public functions. Google-style docstrings; the API reference is rendered from them.
  • Small pull requests with one purpose. A model integration and a refactor of the processor are two pull requests.
  • Vendored model code under tabtune/models/<name>/ is not edited. If upstream has a bug, work around it in tabtune_support.py and link the upstream issue.
  • A change to public behaviour comes with a test and a line in CHANGELOG.md under Unreleased.

docs.title: Adding a model
docs.text:
1. Vendor the upstream tree under tabtune/models/<name>/, keep its LICENSE, rewrite its absolute imports to the vendored path, and change nothing else.
  2. Write tabtune/models/<name>/tabtune_support.py: an estimator that accepts TabTune's constructor conventions (device, model_path, tuning_strategy), exposes the torch module for LoRA, and, if the model fine-tunes, the episode loss and validation hooks the episodic driver needs.
  3. Add a preprocessor in tabtune/Dataprocess/ only if the default is wrong for the model. Models that preprocess internally get a pass-through.
  4. Register a ModelSpec in tabtune/registry/catalog.py: tasks, strategies, modes, the capability envelope, the weight licence with its URL, and the paper.
  5. Add the dispatch branch in tabtune/TuningManager/tuning.py and, if LoRA applies, an entry in MODEL_LORA_TARGETS in peft_utils.py.
  6. Add docs/models/<name>.md (copy the structure of an existing page) and a row in the nav in mkdocs.yml.
  7. Add tests/test_<name>_integration.py that runs inference, fine-tuning and LoRA on a tiny randomly initialised network, and bump the registry count in tests/test_registry.py and tests/test_TimeSeries_registry.py.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
pip install -r requirements-docs.txt
mkdocs serve            # http://127.0.0.1:8000
mkdocs build --strict   # what the CI runs

Pages are Markdown under docs/, built with mkdocs-material. Sentence case for headings, runnable examples, no claims the code does not back. If you change a public signature, change the page that documents it in the same pull request.

docs.title: Pull requests
docs.text:
• Open an issue first for anything larger than a fix, so the design is agreed before the code exists.
  • Describe what changed and why, and paste the test output.
  • One approving review and green CI merge it. Maintainers may squash.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
• Bugs and feature requests: GitHub Issues.
  • Questions: Discord.
  • Security problems: see SECURITY.md. Please do not file them as public issues.

By contributing you agree that your contribution is licensed under the MIT License that covers the project. Vendored model code keeps its own licence.

docs.title: What is TabTune, in one sentence?
docs.text: One scikit-learn style pipeline for running and fine-tuning 24 tabular foundation models, plus a matching pipeline for eleven time series foundation models, with the model code vendored and the licences checked before anything downloads. See Home.

docs.title: Do I need a GPU?
docs.text: Not for inference on the smaller models (TabPFN v2, TabICL, Orion-MSP, EXAONE, Kumo small): a few thousand rows predict in seconds on CPU. Fine-tuning anything, or inference with the large models on large tables, wants a GPU.

docs.title: Which Python version?
docs.text: 3.10 or newer. Toto 2 needs 3.12. See Installation.

docs.title: Do I have to install each model's package?
docs.text: No. The model code is vendored under tabtune/models/; pip install -e . is the whole install. Checkpoints download from the Hugging Face Hub on the first fit().

docs.title: Does TabTune support regression?
docs.text: Yes, on every model with a regression head: the TabPFN family, TabICL v2, Mitra and Mitra v2, ConTextTab, TabDPT, LimiX and LimiX-2, TabFM, xRFM, iLTM, EXAONE (local checkpoint), Causilo, TabLDM and Kumo. TabICL, Orion-MSP and Orion-BiX are classification only. list_models(task="regression") is the live answer. See Regression.

docs.title: inference, finetune or peft?
docs.text: Start with inference; it is a real baseline for an in-context model. Move to peft when you have a GPU and more than a few thousand rows, and to finetune when memory allows and peft plateaued. For Kumo, LimiX-2 and TabAbax the fine-tuning loop validates itself and keeps the pretrained weights if nothing beats them. For the others, hold out a test set and compare. See Tuning Strategies and Validated Fine-Tuning.

docs.title: Which models can I use commercially?
docs.text: The weights decide. list_models(commercial_ok=True) returns them, and TabularPipeline(..., license_mode="commercial") refuses the rest at construction time. The table is on Models.

docs.title: Why did fine-tuning make my model worse?
docs.text: Because an in-context model is already adapted to your data at prediction time, and a training loop that does not measure itself against that baseline can drift away from it. The Validated Fine-Tuning page explains the causes and the fix. If finetune_report_.kept says "pretrained", zero-shot won and that is the honest result.

docs.title: How do I pick a model for my dataset?
docs.text: Rows, columns, classes, text, licence, hardware, in that order; then a Leaderboard over the survivors. The checklist is at the bottom of Models and the long version is Model Selection.

docs.title: My dataset has 50,000 rows and TabPFN warns. Is the result wrong?
docs.text: No, it is a soft limit: TabTune passes ignore_pretraining_limits=True, so the model runs and accuracy degrades past 10,000 rows. For big tables use TabPFN v3 or v3.5, TabICL v2, Kumo or TabDPT, or subsample the context. envelope_mode="error" turns the warning into an exception if you would rather be stopped.

docs.title: Can I use my own preprocessing?
docs.text: Yes. processor_params overrides imputation, scaling and encoding; Custom Preprocessing shows how to put your own transformer in the chain. Models that preprocess internally (Kumo, LimiX-2, TabAbax, TabPFN v3.5, Causilo, TabLDM) receive the raw frame regardless.

docs.title: Does the time series pipeline fine-tune?
docs.text: All eleven foundation models: finetune for every weight, peft for LoRA adapters. The tabular forecasters and the baselines are inference-only. See Time Series Fine-Tuning.

docs.title: Where do I report a bug or ask a question?
docs.text: GitHub Issues for bugs and requests, Discord for questions. Contributing has the workflow, Security is for vulnerabilities.

docs.title: Known Issues
docs.text: Found by reading the code and running the suites, not by trusting earlier docs. Organised by how much each should worry you.

docs.title: Looks like it works, but does less than you think
docs.text:
• The older episodic fine-tuning loop does not validate. For TabICL, Orion-MSP, Orion-BiX, Mitra, TabDPT, TabFM, iLTM and EXAONE, finetune and peft train for the requested epochs and keep the final weights. On the Kumo and LimiX-2 benchmark that loop made every fine-tuned run worse than zero-shot. Those two and TabAbax now use the validated driver; for the others, compare against an inference pipeline on a held-out split before trusting a fine-tuned one.
  • EXAONE's peft is a full fine-tune. Its projections are raw nn.Parameter tensors applied through F.linear, so the LoRA injector wraps zero adapters and the run proceeds with every weight trainable. The log says so; the memory profile is finetune's.
  • xRFM's peft is not LoRA. It is low-rank adaptation of the learned feature matrix. Different thing, same strategy name.
  • PEFT on TabPFN v2 and ConTextTab is experimental. Adapters attach, but training can be unstable. The registry flags it; use finetune if a run misbehaves.
  • TabAbax and LimiX-2 refuse to fine-tune above ten classes. Inference handles more (hierarchical classification in TabAbax), fine-tuning is limited to the head's native class count. The error is explicit.
  • Kumo Tabular above ten classes uses ECOC, one forward per codebook row, so inference cost grows with the class count.

docs.title: Setup and environment
docs.text:
• TabPFN v2.6 and later, TabFM, ConTextTab, EXAONE, Causilo and LimiX-2 weights are non-commercial, and TabLDM, TabDPT, TiRex, TiRex-2 and Time-MoE are unverified. license_mode="commercial" refuses the first group and warns on the second; it cannot read a licence you have negotiated separately, so use license_mode="ignore" in that case.
  • TabFM needs typeguard 2.x. Its vendored estimator decorates functions with jaxtyping.jaxtyped(typechecker=typeguard.typechecked), and typeguard 3 and 4 parse jaxtyping's shape strings as Python and raise SyntaxError at import. 0.2.2 pins typeguard>=2.13.3,<3; an environment that upgrades typeguard breaks TabFM.
  • Toto 2 needs Python 3.12 and its own extra (tabtune[toto2]). On 3.11 the extra installs only with --ignore-requires-python.
  • Time-MoE does not accept NaN in the history. Impute first (the pipeline's imputation task with another model works) or pick another model; the registry records native_missing=False.
  • EXAONE regression needs a locally supplied checkpoint. Only the classification weights are published.
  • skrub is a core dependency since TabPFN v3.5 and is capped at <0.11; a newer skrub in the same environment breaks the v3.5 text and datetime preprocessing.
  • Long fine-tuning runs fragment CUDA memory. PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True helps; see Memory Optimization.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
• The capability and licence tables on Models and Time Series Models are generated from the registry at the time the docs were built. The registry is the source of truth; query it if a number matters.
  • The example notebooks on Notebooks predate the time series pipeline and the validated fine-tuning loop; the examples/ scripts in the repository are current.

If you find something that belongs here, open an issue.

docs.title: License
docs.text:
TabTune's own code is released under the MIT License; the text is in LICENSE at the repository root.

Vendored model code keeps its own licence, in the LICENSE file of its folder under tabtune/models/. Weight licences differ from code licences and are recorded per checkpoint in the registry; license_mode="commercial" checks them before any download. The Models page has the full table, and each model page has the details. The short version:

Licence Models Apache-2.0 or MIT, commercial use fine TabPFN v2 (with attribution), TabICL, TabICL v2, Orion-MSP, Orion-MSP v1.5, Orion-BiX, Mitra, Mitra v2, iLTM, xRFM, Kumo Tabular (OpenMDW-1.1 weights), LimiX v1 (with attribution), Chronos family, Toto 1 and 2 Non-commercial weights TabPFN v2.6, v3, v3.5 and v3.5-fast, TabFM, ConTextTab, EXAONE Tabular, Causilo, LimiX-2, TimesFM 3 Unverified, read the terms TabLDM, TabDPT, TiRex, TiRex-2, Time-MoE

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text: TabTune does not keep a separate roadmap document. These are the gaps that are visible in the code and the Changelog, in one place. If you want to work on one, check Contributing first and search the open issues: someone may be on it.

docs.title: Known gaps
docs.text:
• The validated fine-tuning loop covers three models. Kumo, LimiX-2 and TabAbax use it. TabICL, the Orion-MSP family, Orion-BiX, Mitra, TabDPT, TabFM, iLTM and EXAONE still run the older unvalidated episodic loop, which trains for the requested epochs and keeps the result whether or not it beat zero-shot. Porting them is mostly a matter of supplying an episode loss and a validation hook per model.
  • PEFT on TabPFN v2 and ConTextTab is experimental, and TabPFN v2.6 has no LoRA target table at all.
  • EXAONE regression needs a locally supplied checkpoint; LG AI Research publishes only the classification weights.
  • The tabular side has no command line. tabtune has the timeseries group only.
  • Tabular models as forecasters are inference-only. Fine-tuning a TabularTS-* model on series data means building the table yourself.
  • Conformal coverage on time series is approximate and documented as such; a block-aware or adaptive conformal method would tighten it.
  • No published real-weight benchmark table on this site. examples/22 and examples/timeseries/benchmark.py produce one on your hardware; publishing one needs a fixed GPU and a fixed set of datasets.

docs.title: Recently shipped
docs.text: See the Changelog. Most recently: LimiX-2, Kumo Tabular and TabAbax on the validated fine-tuning driver, and Timestral and T0 for time series; before that, the time series pipeline with nine vendored models, and TabPFN v3.5, Causilo, TabLDM and Mitra v2.

docs.text: Version Supported 0.2.x yes < 0.2.0 no

docs.title: Reporting a vulnerability
docs.text:
Please do not report security vulnerabilities through public GitHub issues.

Email security@lexsi.ai with:

  1. a description of the problem,
  2. steps to reproduce it,
  3. the impact as you understand it,
  4. the affected versions, if you know them,
  5. a suggested fix, if you have one.

You will get an acknowledgement within three working days and a status update within fourteen. We ask that you give us reasonable time to fix the problem before disclosing it, and we will credit you in the release notes unless you prefer otherwise.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: TabTune downloads model checkpoints from the Hugging Face Hub and loads them with safetensors or torch.load. Checkpoints are code-adjacent data; load only checkpoints from sources you trust, and pin them with model_params={"model_path": ...} in production. Vendored model code under tabtune/models/ is covered by this policy; the upstream projects it was copied from have their own.

docs.title: Basic Concepts
docs.text: The vocabulary every other page assumes. Four objects, two tasks, three strategies.

docs.title: TabularPipeline: the object you instantiate
docs.text:
TabularPipeline(
    model_name="TabICL",            # any registry name or alias
    task_type="classification",     # or "regression"
    tuning_strategy="inference",    # "inference" | "finetune" | "peft"
    tuning_params={...},            # epochs, learning_rate, peft_config, finetune_mode ...
    processor_params={...},         # overrides for the DataProcessor
    model_params={...},             # passed to the model constructor
)

It owns a DataProcessor, a TuningManager and the model, and exposes the scikit-learn verbs: fit, predict, predict_proba, evaluate, save, load. Regression adds predict_quantiles and predict_intervals. Three keyword-only arguments control the guards: envelope_mode, license_mode and cache. The full signature is on the TabularPipeline page.

docs.title: DataProcessor: preprocessing that depends on the model
docs.text: Tabular foundation models disagree about input. TabPFN wants integer-encoded categoricals and tolerates NaN; ConTextTab wants the raw strings because it embeds them; Mitra wants no NaN at all; Kumo, LimiX-2 and TabAbax run their own preprocessing inside the model and want the frame untouched. DataProcessor resolves this per model through a preprocessor key in the registry (tabpfn_special, contexttab_special, kumo_special and so on), so you pass the same DataFrame every time. You can still override imputation, scaling and encoding with processor_params. See Data Processing.

docs.title: TuningManager: the strategy dispatcher
docs.text:
fit() hands the preprocessed data and the model to the TuningManager, which runs the chosen strategy:

Strategy What happens in fit() When inference Nothing trains. The training rows become the in-context support set. Baselines, small data, no GPU. finetune Every parameter updates. Modes: meta-learning (episodes), sft (one split), turn_by_turn (regression), native (the vendor's loop). You have a GPU and more than a few thousand rows. peft LoRA adapters train; the base weights stay frozen. Same gains as finetune at a fraction of the memory.

Each model declares which strategies and modes it supports; the registry refuses the rest before anything loads. See Tuning Strategies.

docs.title: The registry: facts about a checkpoint without loading it
docs.text:
tabtune.registry is a torch-free table of ModelSpec records. Each one carries the model's tasks, strategies, fine-tuning modes, a CapabilityEnvelope (class, feature, row and cell limits; whether it reads NaN, text or categoricals natively) and a LicenseSpec for the weights.

from tabtune.registry import list_models, get_model_spec

[s.name for s in list_models(task="regression", strategy="peft", commercial_ok=True)]
get_model_spec("Kumo").license.name     # 'OpenMDW-1.1 (weights) / Apache-2.0 (code)'

The pipeline consults it in its constructor, which is why a licence problem or a class-count mismatch fails in milliseconds and not after a multi-gigabyte download. See Model Registry.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text: classification (binary and multiclass) and regression. The registry says which models support which; TabICL, Orion-MSP and Orion-BiX are classification only. Time series has its own pipeline and its own tasks (forecasting, anomaly detection, imputation, embedding); see Time Series.

docs.title: In-context learning, in one paragraph
docs.text: Most models here are in-context learners. They were pretrained on millions of synthetic tables to predict query rows given labelled support rows, in a single forward pass. At inference, your training set is the support set and your test rows are the queries. No weights change. Fine-tuning these models means training on episodes that look like that forward pass: a support set and a query set sampled from your data. That is what finetune_mode="meta-learning" does, and it is why the support size, the query size and whether the episode resembles the inference context all matter. The Validated Fine-Tuning page explains how the newer loop keeps the result at least as good as zero-shot.

docs.title: The lifecycle
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Choose model<br/>registry] --> B[Construct pipeline<br/>envelope + licence check]
    B --> C[fit<br/>preprocess, then strategy]
    C --> D[predict / evaluate<br/>metrics, calibration, fairness]
    D --> E[save / load]
    D --> F[Compare: leaderboard<br/>Combine: ensemble<br/>Compress: distill]
