docs.title: tabtune.evaluation.metrics
docs.text:
Shared metric computation.

Every metric TabTune reports is computed here. Before this module the same formulas were reimplemented in TabularPipeline.evaluate, the distillation analysis package and the ensemble strategies, and they had already drifted (two different expected-calibration-error implementations with different binning).

Centralising them means a metric added here appears in evaluate(), the leaderboard, the benchmark CSV and the shift report at once.

All functions are pure, take numpy-compatible inputs and never raise on degenerate input: an undefined metric returns float('nan') rather than blowing up a benchmark sweep halfway through.

docs.title: FunctionalWeightLoRALinear
docs.text:
Bases: LoRALinear

LoRA wrapper for leaves read as layer.weight instead of called.

LoRALinear adds its delta in forward. A caller that only takes the weight tensor - F.linear(x, self.out_proj.weight, self.out_proj.bias), or a functional attention call - never runs that, so the adapters would have no effect at all. Merging the delta into weight covers both consumption styles and stays differentiable in the adapters.

The merge is recomputed per read, which is an r x out x in matmul: cheap next to the attention it feeds.

docs.title: inject_custom_lora_into_linear_layers(model: nn.Module, target_names: Optional[Sequence[str]] = None, r: int = 8, alpha: int = 16, dropout: float = 0.0, exclude_patterns: Optional[Sequence[str]] = None, functional_weight_patterns: Optional[Sequence[str]] = None) -> nn.Module
docs.text:
Inject LoRA adapters into linear layers, optionally excluding certain patterns.

Leaves matching functional_weight_patterns get :class:FunctionalWeightLoRALinear instead of :class:LoRALinear, for modules whose weight is consumed as a tensor rather than by calling them.

docs.title: uncertainty_report(X_test: pd.DataFrame, y_test: pd.Series, *, X_cal: Optional[pd.DataFrame] = None, y_cal: Optional[pd.Series] = None, alpha: float = 0.1, n_bins: int = 15, method: str = 'lac') -> Dict[str, float]
docs.text:
Summarise this pipeline's uncertainty behaviour in one dict.

The one-line entry point to :mod:tabtune.uncertainty. Constructing the wrappers by hand stays available and is what you want to keep a calibrated :class:~tabtune.uncertainty.ConformalClassifier around for reuse; this covers the report-once case.

For classification the calibration block (ece, mce, brier) is always computed, and it agrees with :meth:evaluate by construction because both reuse :func:tabtune.evaluation.metrics.calibration_metrics. When a calibration split is also given, a conformal predictor is fitted on it and evaluated on the test split, adding coverage, avg_set_size, sscs (size-stratified coverage - the honest conditional-coverage diagnostic) and alpha. For regression the calibration split is required and the report contains coverage, avg_width and alpha instead.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default X_test DataFrame

Held-out test features the report is computed on.

required y_test Series

Test labels/targets.

required X_cal Optional[DataFrame]

Optional calibration features. Must be disjoint from both the training and test data, or the conformal guarantee is void.

None y_cal Optional[Series]

Optional calibration labels/targets.

None alpha float

Target miscoverage for the conformal block; alpha=0.1 asks for 90% coverage.

0.1 n_bins int

Confidence buckets for ECE/MCE.

15 method str

Conformal score for classification: 'lac' (smallest sets) or 'aps' (adaptive sets).

'lac'

Returns:

Type Description Dict[str, float]

Metric mapping as described above.

Raises:

Type Description RuntimeError

If called before :meth:fit.

ValueError

If only one of X_cal/y_cal is given, or for a regression pipeline without a calibration split.

Example

pipe = TabularPipeline("TabICLv2").fit(X_train, y_train) pipe.uncertainty_report(X_test, y_test, ... X_cal=X_cal, y_cal=y_cal) {'ece': 0.061, 'mce': 0.19, 'brier': 0.31, 'coverage': 0.905, 'avg_set_size': 1.4, 'sscs': 0.77, 'alpha': 0.1}

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: TabularPipeline provides a scikit-learn-compatible interface for training and using tabular foundation models. It coordinates data preprocessing, model initialization, training, and inference.

docs.title: TabularPipeline.__init__()
docs.text:
TabularPipeline(
    model_name: str,
    task_type: str = 'classification',
    tuning_strategy: str = 'inference',
    tuning_params: dict | None = None,
    processor_params: dict | None = None,
    model_params: dict | None = None,
    model_checkpoint_path: str | None = None,
    finetune_mode: str | None = None,
    *,
    cache: str | bool | None = None,        # new in 0.2.0
    envelope_mode: str = 'warn',            # new in 0.2.0
    license_mode: str = 'research',         # new in 0.2.0
    validate: bool = True,                  # new in 0.2.0
)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
model_name (str, required) - Model name or alias. 24 models are registered. - Resolution ignores case, hyphens, underscores, dots and whitespace, so 'TabPFN-v2.6' and 'tabpfnv26' are equivalent. - Canonical names: 'TabPFN', 'TabPFNv26', 'TabPFNv3', 'TabICL', 'TabICLv2', 'OrionMSP', 'OrionMSPv1.5', 'OrionBix', 'Mitra', 'ContextTab', 'TabDPT', 'Limix', 'TabFM', 'XRFM', 'ILTM', 'EXAONETabular' - Do not hardcode this list, call tabtune.registry.list_model_names(). - Example: model_name="TabICLv2"

task_type (str, default: 'classification') - Type of machine learning task. - Supported: 'classification', 'regression' - Regression is supported for: TabPFN, TabPFNv26, TabPFNv3, TabICLv2, Mitra, ContextTab, TabDPT, Limix, TabFM, XRFM, ILTM, EXAONETabular - Classification-only: TabICL, OrionMSP, OrionMSPv1.5, OrionBix - Query it instead of memorising it: [s.name for s in list_models(task="regression")] - Example: task_type="regression"

tuning_strategy (str, default: 'inference') - Training/fine-tuning strategy to use. - Options: - 'inference': Zero-shot predictions (no training) - 'finetune': Full fine-tuning of all parameters - 'peft': Parameter-efficient fine-tuning with LoRA adapters - Example: tuning_strategy="peft"

tuning_params (dict, optional) - Hyperparameters for training/inference. - Common parameters for all models: - device (str): 'cuda' or 'cpu' (default: auto-detected) - epochs (int): Number of training epochs - learning_rate (float): Learning rate for optimizer - batch_size (int): Batch size for training - show_progress (bool): Show tqdm progress bar - save_checkpoint_path (str): Path to save fine-tuned weights - checkpoint_dir (str): Directory for automatic checkpoint saving - weight_decay (float): AdamW weight decay - clip_grad_norm (float): Gradient clipping norm - Episodic training parameters (meta-learning / TBT): - support_size (int): Support set size per episode - query_size (int): Query set size per episode - n_episodes (int): Episodes per epoch (classification) - steps_per_epoch (int): Steps per epoch (regression TBT) - context_size (int): Alias for support_size (regression TBT) - PEFT parameters: - peft_config (dict): LoRA configuration, r, lora_alpha, lora_dropout, target_modules

  • Example: 
    tuning_params={
    "device": "cuda",
    "epochs": 5,
    "learning_rate": 2e-5,
    "batch_size": 8
}

processor_params (dict, optional) - Parameters for data preprocessing. - Common parameters: - imputation_strategy (str): 'mean', 'median', 'mode', 'knn' - scaling_strategy (str): 'standard', 'minmax', 'reliable' - categorical_encoding (str): Encoding method (auto-selected for model-specific) - resampling_strategy (str): 'smote', 'random_oversample', etc. - Example: 

processor_params={
    "imputation_strategy": "median",
    "scaling_strategy": "standard"
}

model_params (dict, optional) - Direct parameters passed to the model constructor. - Model-specific (see individual model documentation). - Example for TabICL: 

model_params={"n_estimators": 16, "softmax_temperature": 0.9}

model_checkpoint_path (str, optional) - Path to a pre-trained model checkpoint (.pt file). - If provided, loads weights from checkpoint instead of default pre-trained weights. - Example: model_checkpoint_path="./checkpoints/tabicl_epoch5.pt"

finetune_mode (str, default: 'meta-learning') - Fine-tuning mode for models that support it. - Options: - 'meta-learning': Episodic meta-learning (default) - 'sft': Standard supervised fine-tuning - Example: finetune_mode="sft"

docs.title: Keyword-only parameters
docs.text:
cache (str | bool | None, default: None) - Prediction cache: 'memory', 'disk', None, or a PredictionCache instance. - Enabling it collapses evaluate()'s three redundant forward passes into one. - Entries are keyed on a fingerprint covering the fitted model and the input data, so refitting or changing the data invalidates automatically. - Inspect with pipeline.cache.stats; clear with pipeline.clear_cache(). - See Prediction Caching.

envelope_mode (str, default: 'warn') - How to treat data outside the model's documented limits: 'error', 'warn', 'ignore'. - Architectural limits (max_classes, min_rows) always raise unless this is 'ignore'. - Resource limits (max_rows, max_features, max_cells) warn under 'warn'.

license_mode (str, default: 'research') - 'research', no licence enforcement. - 'commercial', raise LicenseError on weights that forbid commercial use. - 'ignore', skip the check entirely. - Unverified licences warn under 'commercial' rather than blocking.

validate (bool, default: True) - Check model / task / strategy against the registry before loading weights. - Set False to use a model TabTune does not know about.

pipeline = TabularPipeline(
    model_name="TabICLv2",
    tuning_strategy="finetune",
    cache="disk",
    envelope_mode="error",
    license_mode="commercial",
)
print(pipeline.cache.stats)   # hits / misses / stores / hit_rate

See Model Registry.

docs.title: Raises
docs.text:
Exception When ModelNotFoundError model_name does not resolve to a registered model UnsupportedTaskError Model has no head for task_type UnsupportedStrategyError Model does not implement tuning_strategy EnvelopeError Data violates a hard architectural limit LicenseError Weight licence forbids the intended use under license_mode

All derive from tabtune.registry.TabTuneError.

docs.title: .uncertainty_report(X_test, y_test, *, X_cal=None, y_cal=None, alpha=0.1, n_bins=15, method='lac')
docs.text:
New in 0.2.0. One call for calibration and conformal coverage diagnostics.

report = pipeline.uncertainty_report(
    X_test, y_test,
    X_cal=X_cal, y_cal=y_cal,
    alpha=0.1,          # 90% target coverage
    n_bins=15,          # calibration bins
    method='lac',       # 'lac' | 'aps'
) -> dict

Returns ece, mce, brier, coverage, avg_set_size and sscs (size-stratified coverage, the worst-covered stratum). Omitting X_cal / y_cal gives the calibration metrics only.

The calibration split must be disjoint from training

For an in-context model the training data is the support set. A re-used training frame is detected by fingerprint and raises rather than silently voiding the guarantee.

See Uncertainty Quantification.

docs.title: Common exceptions
docs.text:
RuntimeError: "You must call fit() before predict()" - Cause: Calling predict/evaluate before fitting - Solution: Call .fit() first

ModelNotFoundError: "Unknown model 'X'" - Cause: The name does not resolve to a registered model - Solution: Check tabtune.registry.list_model_names(); the error suggests the closest match

UnsupportedTaskError / UnsupportedStrategyError - Cause: The model has no head for that task, or does not implement that strategy - Solution: get_model_spec(name).tasks and .strategies_for(task)

EnvelopeError: "X supports at most N classes (found M)" - Cause: Data violates a hard architectural limit of the checkpoint - Solution: Pick a model with a larger envelope, or envelope_mode='ignore' if you know what you are doing

RuntimeError: "CUDA out of memory" - Cause: Insufficient GPU memory - Solution: Use PEFT, reduce batch size, or use CPU

docs.title: tabtune.registry.registry
docs.text:
Model registry: lookup, filtering and request validation.

This module turns the declarative catalog into behaviour. It answers three kinds of question:

  1. Resolution - "what does the string 'tabpfn-v2.6' refer to?"
  2. Discovery - "which models support regression and can be shipped commercially?"
  3. Validation - "is this (model, task, strategy, data) combination valid, and if not, what should the user do instead?"

The registry is deliberately free of heavy imports. Importing it costs a few milliseconds and does not pull in torch, so the CLI, documentation build and license checks all stay fast.

None means "no declared limit"; it is deliberately distinct from a large number, because TabTune should not invent limits it has not verified.

docs.title: tabtune.registry.errors
docs.text:
Exception hierarchy for TabTune.

Every error TabTune raises deliberately derives from :class:TabTuneError, so callers can catch the whole family with a single except while still being able to discriminate on the specific failure mode.

The messages here are written to be actionable: when a model cannot be used for a request, the error names the concrete alternatives rather than only stating what went wrong.

docs.title: TabTuneError
docs.text:
Bases: Exception

Base class for every error raised by TabTune.

docs.title: ConfigError
docs.text:
Bases: TabTuneError, ValueError

Raised when a configuration object fails validation.

Subclasses :class:ValueError for backward compatibility: TabTune previously raised bare ValueError for bad configuration, and existing user code that catches ValueError keeps working.

docs.title: ModelNotFoundError
docs.text:
Bases: TabTuneError, ValueError

Raised when a model name does not resolve to a registered model.

docs.title: UnsupportedTaskError
docs.text:
Bases: TabTuneError, ValueError

Raised when a model does not implement the requested task type.

docs.title: UnsupportedStrategyError
docs.text:
Bases: TabTuneError, ValueError

Raised when a model does not implement the requested tuning strategy.

docs.title: EnvelopeError
docs.text:
Bases: TabTuneError, ValueError

Raised when input data exceeds a model's hard capability limits.

These are architectural properties of the pretrained checkpoint (for example TabFM's ten-class output head), not configuration mistakes, so the message points at compatible models rather than at a parameter to change.

docs.title: LicenseError
docs.text:
Bases: TabTuneError, ValueError

Raised when a model's weight license forbids the requested usage mode.

TabTune's license metadata is a convenience for catching obvious mismatches early. It is not legal advice, and the authoritative text always lives upstream.

docs.title: __init__(model_name: str, task_type: str = 'forecasting', tuning_strategy: str = 'inference', tuning_params: dict | None = None, model_params: dict | None = None, forecast_params: dict | None = None, *, task_params: dict | None = None, cache: Any = None, envelope_mode: str = 'warn', license_mode: str = 'research', validate: bool = True) -> None
docs.text:
Build a pipeline around a time series foundation model.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default model_name str

Model name or alias. See :func:tabtune.registry.list_time_series_models; register your own with :func:tabtune.registry.register_time_series_model.

required task_type str

"forecasting" (default), "anomaly_detection", "imputation" or "embedding". :meth:predict returns a :class:ForecastResult, :class:AnomalyResult, :class:ImputationResult or :class:EmbeddingResult.

'forecasting' tuning_strategy str

"inference" (zero-shot), "finetune" (all weights) or "peft" (LoRA adapters), for models whose spec declares them.

'inference' tuning_params dict | None

For zero-shot inference only device and seed apply. Fine-tuning also reads epochs and steps_per_epoch (one step is one batch of sampled windows; default 50 per epoch), learning_rate, batch_size, early_stopping with early_stopping_patience (in epochs), validation_split (any value above 0 holds out the last prediction_length steps of every series), gradient_clip_norm (default 1.0) and, for "peft", peft_config (r, lora_alpha, lora_dropout, target_modules).

None model_params dict | None

checkpoint selects the weights: a validated checkpoint id (defaults to the spec's default_checkpoint) or a local checkpoint directory. device selects the device when tuning_params does not. Other keys are forwarded to the model's adapter.

None forecast_params dict | None

Validated against :class:~tabtune.config.ForecastConfig. prediction_length is required for forecasting; for anomaly detection it is the number of steps forecast from each origin (default 1).

None task_params dict | None

Task options. Anomaly detection: method ("forecast_error", "interval" or "likelihood"), stride, min_context, coverage, alpha, threshold ("conformal", "contamination" or a number), contamination and reference_fraction. Imputation: method ("bidirectional" or "forecast") and min_context.

None cache Any

Result cache: 'memory', 'disk', None or a :class:~tabtune.caching.PredictionCache.

None envelope_mode str

How to treat requests beyond the model's documented limits: 'error', 'warn' (default) or 'ignore'.

'warn' license_mode str

'research' (default), 'commercial' to fail fast on weights that forbid commercial use, or 'ignore'.

'research' validate bool

Check the weight license and restrict checkpoint to the validated list (local directories are always allowed). The model, task and strategy are checked regardless, because the pipeline cannot run anything else.

True

Raises:

Type Description ModelNotFoundError

Unknown model name.

UnsupportedTaskError

The model does not implement task_type.

UnsupportedStrategyError

The model does not support tuning_strategy.

LicenseError

license_mode='commercial' and the weights forbid it.

ConfigError

Invalid forecast_params, tuning_params, task_params, checkpoint, envelope_mode or license_mode.

For zero-shot inference no training happens: fit validates and stores the history and loads the weights. With "finetune" or "peft" the model is then trained on windows sampled from the history; :attr:training_report_ records the run.

docs.text:
Run the pipeline's task on the fitted history or on df.

Forecasting returns prediction_length steps past the end of each series; anomaly detection scores every observation after a warm-up; imputation returns the history with its gaps filled; embedding returns one vector per series.

History in the fitted schema. None uses the history given to :meth:fit. Passing a frame runs the task on new origins or new items without refitting.

None

docs.title: calibrate(df: pd.DataFrame | None = None, *, method: str | None = None, windows: int = 5, step: int | None = None, output_format: str = 'rich') -> TimeSeriesPipeline
docs.text:
Calibrate the forecast quantiles with split conformal prediction.

Forecasts are made from windows rolling origins at the end of the history (or of df), compared with what followed, and the per-horizon-step errors set how much each quantile moves. Later :meth:predict calls return the calibrated quantiles; the point forecast is unchanged. Fitting again removes the calibration.

Use a history the model was not fine-tuned on, or the calibration will be optimistic.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default df DataFrame | None

History to calibrate on, in the fitted schema. None uses the fitted history.

None method str | None

"cqr" (default for models with quantiles), "absolute" (default for point-only models) or "signed". See :mod:tabtune.TimeSeries.calibration.

None windows int

Rolling origins per series.

5 step int | None

Steps between origins (default prediction_length).

None output_format str

'rich' logs a calibration report, 'json' prints its summary as JSON.

'rich'

Returns:

Type Description TimeSeriesPipeline

self.

Raises:

Type Description ConfigError

If the task is not forecasting or no quantile levels were requested.

ValueError

If there are too few calibration rows for the requested levels.

docs.text:
A validated panel of series, ready for a model adapter.

One row is one (item, target) pair: a univariate panel has one row per item, a panel with three targets three consecutive rows per item in schema order. An adapter that forecasts variates jointly recovers the grouping from :meth:item_groups.

Attributes:

Name Type Description item_ids tuple[Hashable, ...]

One identifier per row. (None,) for a single series given without an item column. Repeated across a multivariate item.

values tuple[ndarray, ...]

Per row, the target history as a 1-D float64 array in time order. NaN marks a missing observation; every other value is finite.

last_timestamps tuple[Timestamp, ...]

Per row, the timestamp of the final observation; forecasts start one step after it.

freq str

Pandas frequency string shared by every series.

target_names tuple[str, ...]

Per row, the name of the target column it holds.

past_covariates tuple[Mapping[str, ndarray], ...]

Per row, a mapping of covariate name to a 1-D array as long as that row's history. Shared by the rows of one item.

future_covariates tuple[Mapping[str, ndarray], ...]

Per row, a mapping of covariate name to a 1-D array as long as the forecast horizon. Shared by the rows of one item. Empty unless the schema names known_covariates.

docs.title: tabtune.uncertainty.conformal.ConformalClassifier
docs.text:
Split conformal prediction sets over any probabilistic classifier.

Wraps a fitted pipeline - anything exposing predict_proba - and, after :meth:calibrate on a held-out split, produces prediction sets whose marginal coverage is at least 1 - alpha under exchangeability. The wrapper holds no reference into the pipeline's internals and adds no state to it, so the pipeline stays picklable and reusable.

Two scores are implemented:

  • 'lac' (least ambiguous set-valued classifier): score :math:1 - p_{y}. Produces the smallest sets on average when the model ranks well, but a set can be empty when the threshold q_hat_ is smaller than :math:1 - \max_c p_c for a test point - a confident prediction combined with a small calibration quantile. Empty sets are returned as-is rather than silently patched, because patching would make reported set sizes lie; the marginal guarantee is unaffected.
  • 'aps' (adaptive prediction sets): score is the cumulative probability mass of all classes ranked at or above the true class. Sets adapt to ambiguity - hard examples get larger sets - at the cost of larger sets on average. The randomized tie-breaking of the original paper is off by default for determinism; with randomized=False the top-ranked class is always included, so sets are never empty. Pass randomized=True for the exact-coverage randomized variant, which may produce empty sets.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default pipeline Any

Fitted object with predict_proba. A :class:~tabtune.TabularPipeline.pipeline.TabularPipeline, a scikit-learn classifier, or a fitted :class:~tabtune.uncertainty.Recalibrator.

required method str

'lac' or 'aps'.

'lac' alpha float

Target miscoverage, 0 < alpha < 1. alpha=0.1 asks for 90% coverage.

0.1 randomized bool

APS only - use the randomized score and set rule.

False random_state int | None

Seed for the APS randomization.

None

Attributes:

Name Type Description classes_ ndarray | None

Class labels in probability-column order, set by :meth:calibrate.

n_cal_ int | None

Number of calibration examples.

q_hat_ float | None

The fitted conformal threshold.

Example

conformal = ConformalClassifier(pipeline, alpha=0.1) # doctest: +SKIP conformal.calibrate(X_cal, y_cal) # doctest: +SKIP sets = conformal.predict_set(X_test) # doctest: +SKIP sets.shape # doctest: +SKIP (1000, 3)

.. versionadded:: 0.2.0

docs.title: tabtune.uncertainty.conformal.ConformalRegressor
docs.text:
Split conformal prediction intervals over any regressor.

Two methods:

  • 'absolute': score :math:|y - \hat{y}| around the point prediction, giving symmetric intervals of constant width :math:2 \hat{q}. Works for any regressor with predict.
  • 'cqr' (conformalized quantile regression): scores measure how far the truth escapes the model's own [alpha/2, 1 - alpha/2] quantile band, and the band is widened (or tightened) by the conformal quantile. Interval widths adapt to the input, but the pipeline must expose predict_quantiles - among TabTune models the TabPFN regressor family (v2 to v3.5-fast) and TabICLv2 do (see :meth:~tabtune.TabularPipeline.pipeline.TabularPipeline.predict_quantiles).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default pipeline Any

Fitted regressor. 'absolute' needs predict; 'cqr' additionally needs predict_quantiles(X, quantiles=[...]) returning a mapping from quantile to array.

required method str

'absolute' or 'cqr'.

Target miscoverage, 0 < alpha < 1.

docs.title: tabtune.uncertainty.recalibration.Recalibrator
docs.text:
Learn a post-hoc probability correction on a held-out split.

Two methods:

  • 'temperature': a single scalar T minimising NLL on the calibration split, applied as softmax(log(p) / T). One parameter, so it cannot overfit a small split, and it preserves every prediction; it can only fix global over- or under-confidence. This is the same fit used by :func:tabtune.distillation.strategies.calibrate_student, via the shared :mod:tabtune.uncertainty._scaling.
  • 'isotonic': per-class one-vs-rest isotonic regression followed by row renormalisation, matching the distillation implementation. Each class's mapping is monotone (so per-class ranking is preserved), and it can fix shape as well as scale - at the cost of needing more calibration data to avoid overfitting the step function.

The wrapper is duck-type compatible with the pipeline it wraps, so it composes: ConformalClassifier(Recalibrator(pipe).fit(X_cal, y_cal)) conformalizes the recalibrated probabilities. Use disjoint splits for the two fits - reusing one split makes the conformal threshold optimistic.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default pipeline Any

Fitted object with predict_proba - a :class:~tabtune.TabularPipeline.pipeline.TabularPipeline or any scikit-learn classifier.

required method str

'temperature' or 'isotonic'.

'temperature'

Name Type Description temperature_ float | None

The fitted scalar (temperature method only).

calibrators_ list[Any] | None

Per-class isotonic regressors (isotonic method only).

classes_ ndarray

Class labels in probability-column order, set by :meth:fit.

Example

recal = Recalibrator(pipeline).fit(X_cal, y_cal) # doctest: +SKIP recal.predict_proba(X_test) # doctest: +SKIP recal.temperature_ # doctest: +SKIP 2.31

docs.title: tabtune.uncertainty.report.size_stratified_coverage(set_sizes: np.ndarray, covered: np.ndarray, *, min_stratum: int = _MIN_STRATUM) -> float
docs.text:
Worst-group coverage when test points are stratified by set size.

The definition implemented here: group test points by their exact prediction-set size, compute empirical coverage within each group with at least min_stratum points, and return the smallest group value. A marginally valid conformal predictor can still fail this badly - small sets on examples it wrongly finds easy, large sets elsewhere - and that failure is exactly what marginal coverage cannot see. Values close to the marginal coverage mean the sets adapt honestly; values far below it mean the guarantee is being carried by the easy strata.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default set_sizes ndarray

Prediction-set size per test point, shape (n,).

required covered ndarray

Whether the true label was in the set, shape (n,).

required min_stratum int

Minimum stratum size to include. Strata below it are skipped; if every stratum is below it, the marginal coverage is returned as the honest fallback.

_MIN_STRATUM

Returns:

Type Description float

The worst qualifying stratum's coverage, or nan on empty input.

.. versionadded:: 0.2.0

docs.title: Compare, Combine, Select
docs.text: Three objects and one class method, mirroring the tabular side. Members are TimeSeriesPipeline configurations, so foundation models, tabular forecasters and statistical baselines mix freely.

docs.title: TimeSeriesLeaderboard
docs.text:
from tabtune.TimeSeries import TimeSeriesLeaderboard

board = TimeSeriesLeaderboard(history, schema, forecast_params={"prediction_length": 24}, windows=2)
board.add_models(["SeasonalNaive", "Chronos2", "TiRex", "TabularTS-GBM"])
board.add_model("TiRex", tuning_strategy="peft", tuning_params={"epochs": 2}, label="TiRex LoRA")
board.add_all(commercial_ok=True)        # every registered model that can read the schema
board.run(rank_by="WQL")
board.best()
board.to_markdown("leaderboard.md")

Two modes. Backtest (default): every configuration is fitted on df without its last windows forecast windows and scored on rolling-origin forecasts over them. Holdout: pass df_actual, and every configuration is fitted on df and scored on the observations that follow it. Each entry records the metrics, fit and predict time, the weight licence and, when it failed, the error and the traceback; failed entries rank last instead of hiding.

docs.title: TimeSeriesEnsemble
docs.text:
from tabtune.TimeSeries import TimeSeriesEnsemble

ens = TimeSeriesEnsemble(["ChronosBolt", "TiRex", "SeasonalNaive"],
                         ensemble_strategy="greedy_selection",
                         forecast_params={"prediction_length": 24}, validation_windows=3)
ens.fit(history, schema).predict()
ens.weights_                 # by member label
ens.get_leaderboard()        # each member's validation loss, weight and fit time

Quantiles are combined level by level (Vincentization): the ensemble's q-quantile is a weighted average of the members' q-quantiles. Weights are learned on validation windows at the end of the history.

Strategy Weights mean, median Uniform, or the per-level median. No fitting. weighted_averaging Proportional to one over the validation loss. greedy_selection Caruana et al. ensemble selection with replacement, as in AutoGluon-TimeSeries. The default. stacking Non-negative least squares on the point forecasts. best All weight on the best member.

The validation loss is WQL when quantiles are available and WAPE otherwise.

docs.title: TimeSeriesBenchmark
docs.text:
Several configurations over several datasets, aggregated the way fev-bench does:

  • skill = 1 - geomean(clip(error / baseline error, 0.01, 100)) over tasks, relative to seasonal naive, with a bootstrap interval;
  • win rate: the fraction of tasks a model beats each other model, ties counting one half, averaged over opponents;
  • pairwise tests: Wilcoxon signed-rank tests on task errors with Holm's correction.

A task counts towards the ranking only if every model succeeded on it.

from tabtune.TimeSeries import TimeSeriesBenchmark

bench = TimeSeriesBenchmark(["Chronos2", "TiRex", "SeasonalNaive"], datasets=None)  # None: built-in synthetic sets
results = bench.run()
results.leaderboard(metric="WQL")
results.pairwise_tests()
results.save("bench_out")       # raw.csv, leaderboard.csv, report.md, config.json

The built-in datasets are seeded synthetic panels for smoke tests, not a substitute for GIFT-Eval or fev-bench. Pass your own as {"name": {"df": ..., "schema": ..., "prediction_length": ...}}.

docs.title: TimeSeriesPipeline.select
docs.text:
best = TimeSeriesPipeline.select(history, schema, {"prediction_length": 24},
                                 candidates=["Chronos2", "TiRex", "SeasonalNaive"],
                                 windows=3, rank_by="WQL", license_mode="commercial")
best.predict()

Backtests the candidates and returns the best one already fitted on the full history. license_mode="commercial" drops candidates you could not ship before spending time on them.

docs.title: From the command line
docs.text: tabtune timeseries benchmark --models Chronos2,TiRex,SeasonalNaive --data a.csv --data b.csv --horizon 24 --output bench_out

docs.title: Time Series Fine-Tuning
docs.text:
All eleven foundation models support tuning_strategy="finetune" (every weight) and "peft" (LoRA adapters on the linear layers each adapter names). Training windows are sampled from the history: a context of context_length steps followed by prediction_length steps to predict, so the model trains on the shape it will be asked for.

pipe = TimeSeriesPipeline(
    "TiRex",
    tuning_strategy="peft",
    forecast_params={"prediction_length": 24},
    tuning_params={
        "epochs": 3,
        "steps_per_epoch": 50,
        "learning_rate": 1e-4,
        "batch_size": 32,
        "validation_split": 0.1,          # any value above 0 holds out the last horizon of every series
        "early_stopping": True,
        "early_stopping_patience": 2,
        "peft_config": {"r": 8, "lora_alpha": 16, "lora_dropout": 0.05},
    },
)
pipe.fit(history, schema)
pipe.backtest(windows=3)
pipe.save("tirex-lora.joblib")       # adapters and the fitted state travel with the file

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Key Default Meaning epochs 1 Passes over steps_per_epoch batches. steps_per_epoch 50 One step is one batch of sampled windows. learning_rate 1e-5 AdamW learning rate. batch_size 32 Windows per step. validation_split 0 Above 0 holds out the last prediction_length steps of every series for early stopping. early_stopping, early_stopping_patience off, 1 Stop after this many epochs without validation improvement. gradient_clip_norm 1.0 Gradient-norm clip. device, seed auto, 0 Also the only two keys zero-shot inference reads. peft_config - r, lora_alpha, lora_dropout, target_modules (overrides the adapter's defaults).

forecast_params["context_length"] sets the training context too; None uses the model's limit. A horizon longer than the checkpoint was documented for is trained at the limit and rolled out at prediction time, with a warning.

docs.title: What a fine-tuned pipeline carries
docs.text: save() writes the tuned state: every weight for finetune, only the adapters for peft, plus the schema and the configuration. load() rebuilds the base model from its checkpoint and applies the state, so the saved file stays small for LoRA runs.

docs.title: When it helps
docs.text:
Zero-shot is strong on most public benchmarks, and a fine-tuned run can lose to it. Always backtest() both, or put both on a TimeSeriesLeaderboard with a label:

board = TimeSeriesLeaderboard(history, schema, forecast_params={"prediction_length": 24}, windows=3)
board.add_model("TiRex")
board.add_model("TiRex", tuning_strategy="peft", tuning_params={"epochs": 2}, label="TiRex LoRA")
board.run()

A fine-tuned member on the leaderboard or in an ensemble is trained without the scored windows and refitted on the whole history afterwards, so its score is honest.

docs.title: Time Series Models
docs.text: Eleven time series foundation models, vendored. No model package is installed: the upstream code lives under tabtune/models/ with its licence file and is imported only when a pipeline is fitted. All eleven run zero-shot, fine-tune fully or with LoRA, and serve embeddings. The tables were generated from the registry; query it with list_time_series_models() or tabtune timeseries list-models rather than copying them.

docs.title: Tabular foundation models as forecasters
docs.text: TabPFN-TS re-implements the TabPFN-TS recipe on TabTune's vendored TabPFN v3.5: per-series regression on calendar and Fourier time features, known covariates included, native quantiles. Every tabular model with a regression head is also registered as TabularTS-<name>, with TabPFN-TS's time features or a pooled lag design (model_params={"features": "time" | "lags"}). Today that is 20 models: TabularTS-TabPFN, TabularTS-TabPFNv26, TabularTS-TabPFNv3, TabularTS-TabPFNv35, TabularTS-TabPFNv35Fast, TabularTS-Causilo, TabularTS-TabLDM, TabularTS-TabICLv2, TabularTS-Mitra, TabularTS-MitraV2, TabularTS-ContextTab, TabularTS-TabDPT, TabularTS-Limix, TabularTS-KumoTabular, TabularTS-LimiXv2, TabularTS-TabAbax, TabularTS-TabFM, TabularTS-XRFM, TabularTS-ILTM, TabularTS-EXAONETabular. They inherit the tabular model's weight licence. TabularTS-GBM is a weight-free gradient-boosting forecaster on the same lag design, and any scikit-learn regressor drops in through SklearnBackend. All of these are inference-only as forecasters; see Tabular Models as Forecasters.

docs.title: Statistical baselines
docs.text:
Every leaderboard needs a floor. These have no weights and run anywhere.

Baseline model_name Aliases What it does SeasonalNaive SeasonalNaive seasonal-naive, snaive Repeats the last seasonal cycle; the reference of fev-bench and GIFT-Eval skill scores. Naive Naive random-walk Repeats the last observation. Mean Mean historic-average Forecasts the historical mean. Drift Drift random-walk-drift Extrapolates the line from the first to the last observation. WindowAverage WindowAverage moving-average Forecasts the mean of the last window (one season by default). TabularTS-GBM TabularTS-GBM tabular-gbm Gradient boosting on a pooled direct multi-horizon lag design (M5 style), one quantile-loss model per level.

docs.title: Picking one
docs.text:
• Covariates or several targets? Chronos-2 and Timestral (numeric and categorical covariates), TimesFM 3, T0, Toto 1, TiRex-2 (numeric covariates), or TabPFN-TS (known covariates only).
  • Long histories? Timestral (32,768 steps), TimesFM 3 (15,360), Chronos-2 (8,192), Toto (4,096).
  • Fast and cheap? Chronos-Bolt predicts all quantiles in one pass and is the usual default. TiRex is small and strong on both short and long horizons.
  • Commercial use? Chronos family and Toto are Apache-2.0. TimesFM 3 is non-commercial. TiRex, TiRex-2, Time-MoE, Timestral and T0 are unverified; read their terms.
  • Observability metrics? Toto was trained for them.
  • Any quantile level? T0 interpolates between its trained levels and extrapolates on exponential tails, so any level in (0, 1) is served. Toto samples, which does the same.
  • Not sure? TimeSeriesPipeline.select(...) backtests the candidates and returns the best one, fitted. See Compare, Combine, Select.

docs.title: Time Series
docs.text:
TimeSeriesPipeline is TabularPipeline for sequences: name a model, a task and a tuning strategy, call fit, then predict. The data is a long frame with one row per series and timestamp, and a TimeSeriesSchema names the role of each column. Eleven time series foundation models are vendored, every tabular model with a regression head doubles as a forecaster, and five statistical baselines give every comparison a floor.

from tabtune.TimeSeries import TimeSeriesPipeline, TimeSeriesSchema, make_panel, split_horizon

df = make_panel(n_series=5, length=400, freq="h")           # or your own long frame
schema = TimeSeriesSchema(target="target", item_id="item_id")
history, actual = split_horizon(df, schema, prediction_length=24)

pipe = TimeSeriesPipeline("ChronosBolt", forecast_params={"prediction_length": 24})
forecast = pipe.fit(history, schema).predict()
forecast.to_pandas()      # item_id, timestamp, target, point, 0.1, 0.5, 0.9
pipe.evaluate(actual)     # MAE, RMSE, sMAPE, MASE, pinball, WQL, coverage
pipe.backtest(windows=3)  # rolling-origin scores
pipe.calibrate(windows=4) # conformal intervals, for any model

Swap "ChronosBolt" for "TiRex", "TabPFN-TS" or "SeasonalNaive" and nothing else changes.

docs.title: The input contract
docs.text:
Long format: one row per (item, timestamp) with the target in its own column. Extra targets and covariates are extra columns, named by the schema.

schema = TimeSeriesSchema(
    target=["load", "price"],          # one column, or several for a multivariate forecast
    timestamp="timestamp",             # anything pandas.to_datetime accepts
    item_id="site",                    # None treats the frame as a single series
    freq="h",                          # None infers it and requires every series to agree
    past_covariates=["temperature"],   # observed over the history only
    known_covariates=["promo"],        # also known over the horizon; supplied via future_df
)
pipe = TimeSeriesPipeline("Chronos2", forecast_params={"prediction_length": 24})
pipe.fit(history, schema, future_df=future_promo)
pipe.evaluate(actual)["per_target"]

A model that cannot read a schema feature rejects it with the models that can named in the error. NaN in the history is allowed for every model except Time-MoE, which the registry records.

docs.title: The constructor
docs.text:
TimeSeriesPipeline(
    model_name,                      # registry name or alias
    task_type="forecasting",         # "anomaly_detection" | "imputation" | "embedding"
    tuning_strategy="inference",     # "finetune" | "peft"
    tuning_params=None,              # epochs, learning_rate, batch_size, peft_config ...
    model_params=None,               # checkpoint, device, adapter options
    forecast_params=None,            # prediction_length (required), quantile_levels, context_length
    task_params=None,                # anomaly / imputation options
    cache=None, envelope_mode="warn", license_mode="research", validate=True,
)

model_params["checkpoint"] picks the weights: one of the validated checkpoint ids for the model (the registry lists them) or a local directory. forecast_params["quantile_levels"] asks for quantiles; each adapter maps them onto what its model produces, interpolating inside the grid, clamping outside it with a warning, or refusing a level the model never produced. Quantiles are sorted before they reach you, and forecast.metadata["point_forecast"] says whether the point is a mean or a median.

docs.title: What the pipeline guarantees
docs.text:
• Checks before downloads. The registry confirms the model supports the task and the strategy, license_mode="commercial" refuses non-commercial weights, and envelope_mode warns or errors when the horizon exceeds what the checkpoint was documented for.
  • No configuration is scored on data it was fitted on. backtest, the leaderboard and the ensemble train without the scored windows.
  • Covariates a model cannot read are an error, never silently dropped.
  • Quantiles mean what they say, as above.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
Method What it does fit(df, schema, future_df=None) Validate the history, load the model, train it for finetune and peft. predict(df=None, future_df=None) The task's result for the fitted history, or for a new df. evaluate(df_actual, forecast=None, history=None) MAE, RMSE, sMAPE, MASE, pinball loss, WQL and coverage against observed values; per_target for multivariate schemas. backtest(windows, step=None) Rolling-origin forecasts over the end of the history, scored. calibrate(method="cqr", windows=4) Split conformal calibration of the quantiles, one threshold per horizon step. Methods cqr, absolute, signed. tune_context_length(candidates, windows) Choose context_length by backtest and keep the best. select(df, schema, forecast_params, candidates, ...) Class method: backtest the candidates and return the best one, fitted. save(path) / load(path) Persist the fitted pipeline, adapters included.

Conformal coverage on time series is approximate because consecutive windows are not exchangeable; calibrate() says so in its metadata and evaluate() reports the realised coverage so you can check.

docs.title: Where to next
docs.text:
• Models: the eleven foundation models, the tabular forecasters and the baselines, with context limits, covariate support and licences.
  • Tasks: anomaly detection, imputation and embeddings from the same fitted forecaster.
  • Fine-Tuning: full and LoRA fine-tuning of the foundation models.
  • Compare, Combine, Select: leaderboard, ensemble, benchmark and select().
  • Tabular Models as Forecasters and Series Histories as Features: the two bridges between the tabular and the time series sides.
  • CLI: the same operations from the shell.

docs.title: Series Histories as Features
docs.text:
The other bridge. A customer table, a sensor table, a store table: each row is an entity with a history somewhere else (transactions, readings, sales). SeriesFeaturizer turns that history into features of the row, leak-safe, for any TabularPipeline model.

from tabtune.bridge import SeriesFeaturizer

feat = SeriesFeaturizer(
    transactions,                 # long frame: one row per (customer, date)
    id_col="customer",
    time_col="date",
    cutoff="as_of",               # column of the entity table: the row's own timestamp
    model="TiRex",                # optional: a time series model for embeddings
    n_components=4,               # PCA of the embeddings
)
X = feat.fit_transform(customers)

Each row of customers receives summary statistics of its history (count, mean, standard deviation, trend, last value, recency, and so on) and, when a model is named, a compressed embedding of that history, all computed only from observations at or before the row's own cutoff. A row dated in March never sees April. That is the leak-safety guarantee, and it is why cutoff is required.

add_series_features(entities, history, ...) is the one-call form. The featurizer is a scikit-learn transformer, so it composes with Pipeline and with Custom Preprocessing.

Then it is an ordinary tabular problem:

from tabtune import TabularPipeline

pipe = TabularPipeline("Kumo", task_type="classification", tuning_strategy="inference")
pipe.fit(X_train, y_train)

examples/timeseries/embeddings_and_series_features.py builds the whole thing end to end.

docs.title: Tabular Models as Forecasters
docs.text: A tabular foundation model with a regression head can forecast: build a table where each row is one timestamp of one series with features that describe it, fit the model on the history, predict the horizon rows. TabTune ships two designs for that table and registers every regression-capable tabular model with both.

docs.title: TabPFN-TS
docs.text:
A re-implementation of Prior Labs' TabPFN-TS recipe on TabTune's vendored TabPFN v3.5. Each series is a separate regression problem; the features are calendar components and Fourier terms of the timestamp plus any known covariates. Quantiles come from the model's native regression head.

pipe = TimeSeriesPipeline("TabPFN-TS", forecast_params={"prediction_length": 24,
                                                        "quantile_levels": [0.1, 0.5, 0.9]})
pipe.fit(history, schema, future_df=future_known).predict()

Context up to 32,768 rows, known covariates (numeric and categorical) read, past-only covariates not. The TabPFN 3.5 weight licence applies: non-commercial.

docs.title: TabularTS-<name>
docs.text:
Every tabular model with a regression head, as a forecaster: TabularTS-TabPFN, TabularTS-TabICLv2, TabularTS-Mitra, TabularTS-KumoTabular, TabularTS-LimiXv2, TabularTS-TabAbax and so on, 20 in all. Two feature designs:

TimeSeriesPipeline("TabularTS-TabICLv2", model_params={"features": "time"})   # TabPFN-TS's time features, per series
TimeSeriesPipeline("TabularTS-Mitra",    model_params={"features": "lags"})   # pooled direct multi-horizon lag design, M5 style

With "lags" the series are pooled into one table of lagged values and one model predicts every horizon step directly. Models with native quantiles (TabPFN family, TabICL v2) return them; the others return point forecasts, and calibrate() can wrap intervals around those. Each forecaster inherits its tabular model's weight licence and commercial_use_ok, so list_time_series_models(commercial_ok=True) filters them correctly.

These are inference-only as forecasters; to fine-tune a tabular model on your series, build the table yourself and use TabularPipeline.

docs.title: TabularTS-GBM and scikit-learn
docs.text: TabularTS-GBM is gradient boosting on the pooled lag design, one quantile-loss model per level, with no weights to download. It is a sensible second baseline after seasonal naive, and it is what the lag design looks like without a foundation model. Any scikit-learn regressor drops into the same place through SklearnBackend.

docs.title: When to reach for these
docs.text:
• Many short series with rich calendar structure: TabPFN-TS does well.
  • Strong known covariates (promotions, prices, holidays): the tabular designs read them as columns; several foundation models cannot.
  • A floor for a leaderboard that is better than seasonal naive: TabularTS-GBM.

The script examples/timeseries/tabular_forecasting.py runs the comparison.

docs.title: Time Series Tasks
docs.text:
One fitted forecaster serves four tasks. task_type picks the task; predict() returns a ForecastResult, an AnomalyResult, an ImputationResult or an EmbeddingResult.

from tabtune.TimeSeries import TimeSeriesPipeline

TimeSeriesPipeline("ChronosBolt", task_type="anomaly_detection",
                   task_params={"method": "interval"}).fit(df, schema).predict()
TimeSeriesPipeline("ChronosBolt", task_type="imputation").fit(df_with_gaps, schema).predict()
TimeSeriesPipeline("TiRex", task_type="embedding").fit(df, schema).predict().embeddings

docs.title: Forecasting
docs.text:
The default. forecast_params["prediction_length"] is required; quantile_levels asks for quantiles; context_length caps the history each forecast reads. The result's to_pandas() is the stable public layout: one row per (item, target, timestamp) with point and one column per quantile level.

pipe = TimeSeriesPipeline("Chronos2", forecast_params={"prediction_length": 24,
                                                       "quantile_levels": [0.05, 0.5, 0.95]})
result = pipe.fit(history, schema).predict()
result.point            # [row, horizon], read-only
result.quantiles        # [row, horizon, level]
result.metadata["point_forecast"]   # "mean" or "median"

docs.title: Anomaly detection
docs.text:
Each observation is scored against rolling forecasts made from the history before it, and the scores become conformal p-values against a reference period. alpha is the false alarm rate when the reference is clean.

task_params key Default Meaning method "forecast_error" "forecast_error", "interval" (distance outside the forecast interval) or "likelihood". stride 1 Steps between forecast origins. Larger is faster and coarser. min_context model-specific Observations before scoring starts. coverage 0.98 Interval coverage for "interval". alpha 0.01 False alarm rate for the conformal threshold. threshold "conformal" "conformal", "contamination" or a number. contamination - Expected anomaly fraction for the "contamination" threshold. reference_fraction - Share of the history used as the clean reference.

forecast_params["prediction_length"] is the number of steps forecast from each origin (default 1).

res = TimeSeriesPipeline("ChronosBolt", task_type="anomaly_detection",
                         task_params={"alpha": 0.02}).fit(df, schema).predict()
res.anomalies()                   # only the flagged rows
res.evaluate(labels=df["is_anomaly"])   # AUROC, AUPRC, precision, recall, F1

Evaluate on labelled data before trusting a detector. make_anomalous_panel() makes a seeded panel with known point anomalies for exactly that.

docs.title: Imputation
docs.text:
Each gap is filled by forecasting forward from the values before it and, where there are enough, backward from the values after it (the reversed series), blending the two across the gap. method="forecast" uses the forward pass only. The result keeps the schema's columns with the targets filled, plus an imputed flag and, for a single target, a 10 to 90 percent band of the fill.

filled = TimeSeriesPipeline("Chronos2", task_type="imputation").fit(df_with_gaps, schema).predict()
filled.to_pandas()[["item_id", "timestamp", "target", "imputed", "lower", "upper"]]

docs.title: Embeddings
docs.text:
One vector per (item, target) series from the model's encoder.

emb = TimeSeriesPipeline("TiRex", task_type="embedding").fit(df, schema).predict()
emb.embeddings          # [row, dim]
emb.similarity()        # [row, row] cosine similarity
emb.to_pandas()         # item column, target, emb_0 ... emb_<dim-1>

These are what SeriesFeaturizer adds to a tabular frame.

docs.title: From the command line
docs.text:
tabtune timeseries anomalies --data sensors.csv --model ChronosBolt --alpha 0.02
tabtune timeseries impute    --data sales.csv   --model Chronos2 --output filled.csv
tabtune timeseries embed     --data sales.csv   --model TiRex    --output emb.csv

See CLI.

docs.title: Benchmarking with TabularLeaderboard
docs.text:
Compare models and strategies on the same splits.

from tabtune import TabularLeaderboard

leaderboard = TabularLeaderboard(X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test)

leaderboard.add_model(
    model_name='TabICL',
    tuning_strategy='inference',
    model_params={'n_estimators': 16}
)
leaderboard.add_model(
    model_name='TabICL',
    tuning_strategy='finetune',
    model_params={'n_estimators': 16},
    tuning_params={'epochs': 5, 'learning_rate': 1e-5}
)
leaderboard.add_model(
    model_name='TabPFN',
    tuning_strategy='inference'
)

leaderboard.run(rank_by='roc_auc_score')

docs.title: k-fold cross-validation
docs.text:
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold
import numpy as np
from tabtune import TabularPipeline

def cross_validate(X, y, model_name, params, k=5):
    """Perform k-fold cross-validation."""

    skf = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=k, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
    scores = []
    f1_scores = []

    for fold_idx, (train_idx, val_idx) in enumerate(skf.split(X, y)):
        X_train_fold = X.iloc[train_idx]
        X_val_fold = X.iloc[val_idx]
        y_train_fold = y.iloc[train_idx]
        y_val_fold = y.iloc[val_idx]

        # Train
        pipeline = TabularPipeline(
            model_name=model_name,
            tuning_strategy='finetune',
            tuning_params=params
        )

        pipeline.fit(X_train_fold, y_train_fold)
        metrics = pipeline.evaluate(X_val_fold, y_val_fold)

        scores.append(metrics['accuracy'])
        f1_scores.append(metrics['f1_score'])

        print(f"Fold {fold_idx+1}/{k}: Acc={metrics['accuracy']:.4f}, "
              f"F1={metrics['f1_score']:.4f}")

    print(f"\nMean Accuracy: {np.mean(scores):.4f} ± {np.std(scores):.4f}")
    print(f"Mean F1 Score: {np.mean(f1_scores):.4f} ± {np.std(f1_scores):.4f}")

    return scores, f1_scores

# Usage
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('data.csv')
X = df.drop('target', axis=1)
y = df['target']

scores, f1s = cross_validate(
    X, y,
    model_name='TabICL',
    params={'epochs': 5},
    k=5
)

# Issue: Low accuracy

Eighteen Colab notebooks, one feature each. They download real weights and run on Colab's free GPU tier; the ones that fine-tune are slow on CPU. The examples/ directory in the repository has the same material as plain scripts, listed on Features.

# Notebook What it runs 1 Unified API One TabularPipeline call across several models. Open in Colab 2 Model-aware preprocessing What DataProcessor does per model, and how to override it. Open in Colab 3 Fine-tuning strategies inference, finetune in its modes, and peft, compared. Open in Colab 4 Model comparison TabularLeaderboard over models and strategies. Open in Colab 5 Checkpoint management Save, load, resume. Open in Colab 6 Advanced usage PEFT configuration and hybrid strategies. Open in Colab 7 Resampling Context and support/query sampling. Open in Colab 8 Regression, inference Zero-shot regression. Open in Colab 9 Regression, fine-tuning turn_by_turn and native regression fine-tuning. Open in Colab 10 Evaluation metrics What evaluate() returns and the calibration and fairness reports. Open in Colab 11 Benchmarking Benchmark suites and result handling. Open in Colab 12 TabPFN v2.6 Classification and regression with the native fine-tuning API. Open in Colab 13 TabICL v2 Classification and quantile regression. Open in Colab 14 Ensembling The six TabularEnsemble strategies. Open in Colab 15 Distillation Single and multi-teacher TabDistiller. Open in Colab 16 Causal inference Treatment effects with a TFM as the nuisance learner. Open in Colab 17 EXAONE Tabular End to end with EXAONE. docs.title: Comparing base-FT vs PEFT
docs.text:
import time
import torch
from tabtune import TabularPipeline

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = load_data()

# Method 1: Base Fine-Tuning
print("=== Base Fine-Tuning ===")
torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats()

start = time.time()
pipeline_base = TabularPipeline(
    model_name='TabICL',
    tuning_strategy='finetune',
    tuning_params={'epochs': 5}
)
pipeline_base.fit(X_train, y_train)
base_time = time.time() - start
base_memory = torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() / 1e9

metrics_base = pipeline_base.evaluate(X_test, y_test)

print(f"Time: {base_time:.1f}s")
print(f"Memory: {base_memory:.1f}GB")
print(f"Accuracy: {metrics_base['accuracy']:.4f}")

# Method 2: PEFT
print("\n=== PEFT (LoRA) ===")
torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats()

start = time.time()
pipeline_peft = TabularPipeline(
    model_name='TabICL',
    tuning_strategy='peft',
    tuning_params={
        'epochs': 5,
        'peft_config': {'r': 8}
    }
)
pipeline_peft.fit(X_train, y_train)
peft_time = time.time() - start
peft_memory = torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() / 1e9

metrics_peft = pipeline_peft.evaluate(X_test, y_test)

print(f"Time: {peft_time:.1f}s")
print(f"Memory: {peft_memory:.1f}GB")
print(f"Accuracy: {metrics_peft['accuracy']:.4f}")

# Comparison
print("\n=== Comparison ===")
print(f"Speedup: {base_time/peft_time:.1f}x")
print(f"Memory savings: {(1 - peft_memory/base_memory)*100:.0f}%")
print(f"Accuracy loss: {(metrics_base['accuracy'] - metrics_peft['accuracy'])*100:.2f}%")

            }

    )

else:

        tuning_strategy='peft',
        tuning_params={
            'device': 'cuda',

# Train
pipeline.fit(X_train, y_train)

docs.title: Choosing optimal rank
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from tabtune import TabularPipeline

def evaluate_rank(X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test, rank):
    """Evaluate specific LoRA rank."""

    pipeline = TabularPipeline(
        model_name='TabICL',
        tuning_strategy='peft',
        tuning_params={
            'device': 'cuda',
            'epochs': 3,
            'peft_config': {
                'r': rank,
                'lora_alpha': 2*rank,
                'lora_dropout': 0.05
            }
        }
    )

    pipeline.fit(X_train, y_train)
    metrics = pipeline.evaluate(X_test, y_test)

    return metrics

# Evaluate multiple ranks
ranks = [2, 4, 8, 16, 32]
results = {}

print("Evaluating LoRA ranks...")
for r in ranks:
    print(f"  Testing rank {r}...", end='', flush=True)
    metrics = evaluate_rank(X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test, r)
    results[r] = metrics['accuracy']
    print(f" Accuracy: {metrics['accuracy']:.4f}")

# Find optimal rank
optimal_rank = max(results, key=results.get)
optimal_acc = results[optimal_rank]

print(f"\nOptimal rank: {optimal_rank} (Accuracy: {optimal_acc:.4f})")

# Plot results
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plt.plot(ranks, [results[r] for r in ranks], 'o-', linewidth=2, markersize=8)
plt.xlabel('LoRA Rank')
plt.ylabel('Accuracy')
plt.title('LoRA Rank vs Model Accuracy')
plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.savefig('rank_analysis.png')

docs.title: Cross-validation for regression
docs.text:
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold
import numpy as np
from tabtune import TabularPipeline

def cross_validate_regression(X, y, model_name, params, k=5):

    kf = KFold(n_splits=k, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
    rmse_scores = []
    r2_scores = []

    for fold_idx, (train_idx, val_idx) in enumerate(kf.split(X)):
        X_train_fold = X.iloc[train_idx]
        X_val_fold = X.iloc[val_idx]
        y_train_fold = y.iloc[train_idx]
        y_val_fold = y.iloc[val_idx]

        pipeline = TabularPipeline(
            model_name=model_name,
            task_type='regression',
            tuning_strategy='finetune',
            tuning_params=params
        )

        pipeline.fit(X_train_fold, y_train_fold)
        metrics = pipeline.evaluate(X_val_fold, y_val_fold)

        rmse_scores.append(metrics['rmse'])
        r2_scores.append(metrics['r2_score'])

        print(f"Fold {fold_idx+1}/{k}: RMSE={metrics['rmse']:.4f}, R2={metrics['r2_score']:.4f}")

    print(f"Mean RMSE: {np.mean(rmse_scores):.4f} ± {np.std(rmse_scores):.4f}")
    print(f"Mean R2: {np.mean(r2_scores):.4f} ± {np.std(r2_scores):.4f}")

    return rmse_scores, r2_scores

docs.title: Prediction Caching
docs.text:
Tabular foundation models are expensive to query, and TabTune's own evaluation path used to run three full forward passes for one evaluate() call. Enabling a cache collapses that to one.

from tabtune import TabularPipeline

pipeline = TabularPipeline("TabICLv2", cache="memory")   # or "disk"
pipeline.fit(X_train, y_train)
pipeline.evaluate(X_test, y_test)

print(pipeline.cache.stats)
# hits=2 misses=1 stores=1 hit_rate=67%

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
cache value Backend Lifetime None (default) disabled , "memory" in-process LRU the process "disk" on-disk store across processes a PredictionCache your own instance yours 
from tabtune.caching import PredictionCache

cache = PredictionCache("disk", max_entries=128, cache_dir="./.tabtune-cache")
pipeline = TabularPipeline("TabICLv2", cache=cache)

docs.title: Invalidation is automatic
docs.text:
Entries are keyed on a fingerprint covering the fitted model and the input data, so refitting or changing the data invalidates automatically. There is no stale-cache failure mode to reason about.

from tabtune.caching import fingerprint_data

fingerprint_data(X_test)   # stable hash of the frame

pipeline.cache.stats
# CacheStats: hits=2 misses=1 stores=1 hit_rate=67%

pipeline.cache.stats["hits"]
pipeline.cache.stats.hit_rate
len(pipeline.cache)

docs.text:
pipeline.clear_cache()             # entries removed for this pipeline, returns the count
pipeline.cache.invalidate()        # everything
pipeline.cache.invalidate(scope)   # one scope

docs.title: Where it pays off
docs.text:
Disk caching pays off most where the same test rows are queried repeatedly:

  • Leaderboard runs, many configurations, one test set
  • Shift-evaluation sweeps, folds re-query overlapping rows
  • Uncertainty work, uncertainty_report, recalibration and conformal calibration all read predict_proba on the same frames
  • Notebook iteration, re-running a cell after a predict costs nothing
pipeline = TabularPipeline("TabICLv2", cache="disk")

docs.title: Serialization
docs.text: PredictionCache implements __getstate__ / __setstate__, so a pipeline carrying a cache still pickles. In-memory entries are not written into the pipeline artefact, save() stays the size it was.

docs.title: Lower-level API
docs.text:
from tabtune.caching import PredictionCache, make_cache, CacheStats

cache = make_cache("memory")           # accepts str | bool | None | PredictionCache

value = cache.get_or_compute(
    scope="my-model",
    X=X_test,
    method="predict_proba",
    compute=lambda: expensive_call(X_test),
)

key = PredictionCache.make_key(scope, data_fingerprint, method)
cache.get(key)
cache.set(key, value)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
tabtune.causal does causal inference with a tabular foundation model as the nuisance learner.

The module wraps any TabTune TFM as a nuisance learner inside the standard causal estimators (DoubleML, EconML, DoWhy), so the same models you use for prediction become the engine for double machine learning, meta-learners, and causal forests. It follows the disciplined three-step causal workflow, Identify → Estimate → Refute, and adds first-class sensitive-attribute audits for fairness-critical deployments.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• Six estimators spanning the full spectrum: Double ML (default), S/T/X/R-Learners, and honest Causal Forests.
  • Unified API, the CausalAnalysis class handles every estimator with a consistent, TabularPipeline-style interface.
  • Any TFM as a nuisance learner, TabPFN, TabPFNv26, TabICLv2, Mitra, OrionMSP and TabDPT drop straight in.
  • The full causal discipline, formal identification, effect estimation with confidence intervals, and a battery of refutation checks built in.
  • Fairness audits, proxy detection and counterfactual-fairness checks run alongside refutation, producing a compliance-ready HTML report.
  • Heterogeneous effects, per-row CATE estimation and single-row counterfactual prediction.
  • Multi-model ranking, CausalLeaderboard ranks (estimator × TFM) combinations by stability and refuter pass-rate.
  • Production-grade, complete input validation, graceful degradation when optional backends are missing, verbose logging, and serialisable reports.

docs.title: Estimating a treatment effect with double ML (recommended default)
docs.text:
from tabtune.causal import CausalAnalysis
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

# X must contain the treatment column and every confounder.
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2)

ca = CausalAnalysis(
    model_name="TabPFNv26",          # TFM used as the nuisance learner
    task_type="regression",          # task type of the OUTCOME
    treatment="treated",             # treatment column T
    outcome="outcome",               # outcome column Y (= the y you pass to fit)
    confounders=["age", "income", "score"],
    estimator="dml",                 # Double Machine Learning
    estimator_params={"n_folds": 5, "confidence_level": 0.95},
    tuning_params={"device": "cuda"},
    verbose=True,
)

ca.fit(X_train, y_train)
result = ca.evaluate(X_test, y_test, include=("effect", "refutation"))

print(result["effect"])        # ATE, std error, confidence interval
print(result["refutation"])    # placebo / RCC / subset / sensitivity checks

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
CausalAnalysis (orchestrator)
│
├── fit(X, y)
│   ├── Step 1 - Identify
│   │   ├── GraphBuilder  → DAG (user-supplied / inferred / default)
│   │   └── Identifier    → estimand + adjustment set (DoWhy or fallback)
│   │
│   └── Step 2 - Estimate
│       ├── Build outcome + treatment nuisance learners (TFM → sklearn adapter)
│       ├── Instantiate estimator via ESTIMATOR_REGISTRY[estimator]
│       └── Cross-fit the estimator on the data
│
├── evaluate(X_test, y_test, include=(...))
│   ├── effect                 → ATE / CI / per-level contrasts
│   ├── identification          → estimand report
│   ├── refutation (Step 3)     → Refuter battery
│   ├── proxy                   → ProxyAuditor
│   └── counterfactual_fairness → CounterfactualFairness
│   └── Reporter → rich log + optional HTML model card
│
├── predict_cate(X_query)          → per-row CATE
├── predict_counterfactual(row, …) → single-row what-if
└── evaluate_* (refutation / proxy / counterfactual_fairness / identification)

Every estimator follows the same internal contract: - fit(df), fit nuisance learners and compute the causal estimate. - ate(confidence_level), return ATE, standard error, and confidence interval. - cate(X_query), per-row treatment effects (X/R-Learner, Causal Forest). - counterfactual(row, intervention), single-row counterfactual prediction.

docs.title: The TFM → sklearn bridge
docs.text: Causal libraries expect scikit-learn-style estimators with .fit / .predict / .predict_proba. The _TabTuneSklearnAdapter wraps any TabularPipeline into that interface and is clone-safe, sklearn.clone() round-trips it correctly, which is mandatory because DoubleML and EconML clone nuisance learners internally during cross-fitting. The adapter reports the correct _estimator_type and __sklearn_tags__() so downstream libraries call predict_proba for the treatment model and predict for the outcome model.

docs.title: The causal discipline
docs.text: A predictive model answers "given these features, what is Y?". A causal model answers "if we set T to this value, how does Y change?", a fundamentally harder question that requires assumptions data alone cannot verify. The module enforces the standard three-step discipline that keeps those assumptions explicit.

docs.title: Step 1, identify
docs.text:
Before estimating anything, the module asks whether the effect is even identifiable from the observed data. GraphBuilder constructs a causal DAG (supplied by you, inferred via the PC algorithm, or the canonical "confounders cause T and Y; T causes Y" default). Identifier then derives the estimand, typically a backdoor adjustment set, using DoWhy when installed, or a d-separation fallback otherwise.

If the effect is not identifiable, the module warns loudly and you should treat downstream numbers with caution.

docs.title: Step 2, estimate
docs.text: The chosen estimator fits two nuisance models, one for the outcome E[Y | X] and one for the treatment propensity E[T | X], using your TFM, then combines them into a debiased estimate of the Average Treatment Effect (ATE) with a confidence interval. For multi-level treatments, per-level contrasts are reported.

docs.title: Step 3, refute
docs.text: A point estimate is meaningless without stress tests. The Refuter perturbs the problem and checks the estimate behaves sensibly, a placebo treatment should yield ≈ 0, an injected noise confounder should barely move the estimate, and so on. Refuters that pass don't prove correctness, but refuters that fail prove something is wrong.

docs.title: Estimator reference
docs.text: All estimators are selected via the estimator="..." argument of CausalAnalysis and registered in ESTIMATOR_REGISTRY.

docs.title: Double machine learning (default)
docs.text:
Class: DMLEstimator Estimator key: "dml"

The default and most reliable estimator. Fits an outcome model g(X) = E[Y|X] and a treatment model m(X) = E[T|X], residualises both, and regresses the residuals to recover a Neyman-orthogonal ATE. Cross-fitting removes overfitting bias.

  • Binary / continuous treatment → doubleml.DoubleMLPLR (partially linear regression).
  • Multi-level discrete treatment → doubleml.DoubleMLAPOS (Average Potential Outcomes), reporting one contrast per treatment level.

docs.title: Parameters (estimator_params)
docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description n_folds int 5 Cross-fitting folds n_rep int 1 Repeated cross-fitting rounds confidence_level float 0.95 CI level score str "partialling out" PLR score (binary/continuous T) reference_level numeric smallest level Reference for multi-level contrasts

docs.title: Returns (from ate())
docs.text: ate, std_error, ci_lower, ci_upper, p_value, confidence_level, n_samples, plus per_level and treatment_levels for multi-level treatments.

docs.title: When to use
docs.text: The reliable default. Strongest theoretical guarantees, works for binary, continuous, and multi-level treatments, and is what you should reach for unless you specifically need per-row heterogeneous effects.

docs.title: S-Learner
docs.text:
Class: SLearner Estimator key: "s_learner"

A single model trained on [X, T] with treatment as an extra feature. CATE is the difference between predictions at T=1 and T=0. Simplest meta-learner; can underestimate effects when the treatment signal is weak relative to outcome variance.

Meta-learners (S/T/X/R) currently require a binary {0, 1} treatment. For multi-level treatments use "dml" or "causal_forest".

docs.title: When to use
docs.text: Quick baseline, or when the treatment effect is large and the dataset is small.

docs.title: T-Learner
docs.text:
Class: TLearner Estimator key: "t_learner"

Two models, one per treatment arm. CATE is the difference between the two arms' predictions. Reliable when both arms have ample data; degrades on heavily imbalanced treatments.

docs.title: When to use
docs.text: Balanced treatment assignment with enough data in each arm.

docs.title: X-Learner
docs.text:
Class: XLearner Estimator key: "x_learner"

Propensity-weighted combination of T-Learner residuals, designed specifically for imbalanced treatments. Imputes treatment effects on each arm, then blends them using the propensity score.

docs.title: When to use
docs.text: When one treatment arm is much smaller than the other.

docs.title: R-Learner
docs.text:
Class: RLearner Estimator key: "r_learner"

Residualises both T and Y against X (DML-style), then fits a single CATE model on the residuals via econml.dml.NonParamDML. Strong empirical performance on heterogeneous-effect benchmarks.

docs.title: Parameters (estimator_params)
docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description n_folds int 5 Cross-fitting folds final_model estimator GradientBoostingRegressor Final CATE regressor on residuals

docs.title: When to use
docs.text: When you want a strong CATE estimator and have a moderately sized dataset.

docs.title: Causal Forest
docs.text:
Class: CausalForestEstimator Estimator key: "causal_forest"

An ensemble of honest causal trees (econml.grf.CausalForest) where splits maximise treatment-effect heterogeneity. Honesty (separate samples for splitting and estimation) yields asymptotically unbiased CATE with valid confidence intervals.

docs.title: Parameters (estimator_params)
docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description n_estimators int 200 Number of trees (must be divisible by EconML's subforest_size=4) max_depth int None Max tree depth min_samples_leaf int 5 Minimum leaf size honest bool True Honest splitting random_state int 0 Seed

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: cate(X_query, return_ci=True) returns a dict with point, ci_lower, and ci_upper arrays.

docs.title: When to use
docs.text: Non-parametric heterogeneous effects, especially when you want per-row confidence intervals and don't want to assume a functional form.

docs.title: Refutation reference
docs.text:
Run via evaluate(include=("refutation", ...)) or evaluate_refutation(). The default battery runs four checks; each returns a pass flag and the rule it was judged against.

Check Key What it does Pass rule Placebo treatment placebo Shuffles T so it carries no signal; re-fits \|placebo_ate\| < 0.5 × \|ate\| Random common cause random_common_cause Injects a synthetic noise confounder; re-fits relative ATE shift < 0.2 Data subset subset Re-fits on random subsamples; checks stability coefficient-of-variation < 0.25 Sensitivity sensitivity E-value (VanderWeele & Ding) + Manski bounds E-value ≥ 1.25

The placebo and random-common-cause checks each trigger one estimator refit; the subset check triggers n_subset_iters refits (default 2); the sensitivity check is analytical and triggers zero refits.

Cost note. Each refit re-runs the full cross-fitted estimator, which fits nuisance TFMs n_folds × 2 times (× number of treatment levels for multi-level DML). On a 5-level treatment with n_folds=5, the default battery is roughly 200 TFM fits. Reduce n_folds or pass a smaller checks tuple to speed it up.

docs.title: Refuter run() parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description checks tuple ("placebo", "random_common_cause", "subset", "sensitivity") Which checks to run subset_fraction float 0.7 Fraction sampled per subset refit n_subset_iters int 2 Number of subset refits seed int 0 RNG seed

docs.title: Sensitive-attribute audits
docs.text: Supply sensitive=[...] at construction to enable two fairness audits that run alongside refutation.

docs.title: Proxy auditor
docs.text:
Class: ProxyAuditor

Detects confounders that act as proxies for a sensitive attribute, features that leak protected information even when the sensitive attribute itself is excluded. Each confounder is scored against each sensitive attribute (Spearman for numeric-numeric, eta² for numeric-categorical, Cramér's V for categorical-categorical), and features above threshold (default 0.5) are flagged.

report = ca.evaluate_proxy()
# report["per_attribute"]["gender"]["flagged"] → [{"feature": "zip_code", "score": 0.71}, ...]

docs.title: Counterfactual fairness
docs.text:
Class: CounterfactualFairness

For each row, flips every sensitive attribute to its other observed values (holding everything else fixed) and re-predicts. Reports the flip rate (fraction of rows whose prediction changes) and mean delta (average prediction change). A counterfactually-fair model has a flip rate near zero.

report = ca.evaluate_counterfactual_fairness()
# report["per_attribute"]["gender"] → {"flip_rate": 0.03, "mean_delta": 0.004, ...}

Both audits feed the HTML report when output_path is supplied to evaluate().

docs.text:
CausalAnalysis(
    model_name: str,                  # TFM for the nuisance learner(s)
    task_type: str,                   # "classification" | "regression" (outcome)
    treatment: str,                   # treatment column T
    outcome: str,                     # outcome column Y
    confounders: list[str],           # confounder columns X
    tuning_strategy: str = "inference",
    sensitive: list[str] = None,      # enables fairness audits
    estimator: str = "dml",           # ESTIMATOR_REGISTRY key
    treatment_model: dict = None,     # override the treatment nuisance learner
    estimator_params: dict = None,    # estimator-specific knobs

    processor_params: dict = None,
    model_params: dict = None,
    graph=None,                       # optional networkx.DiGraph
    infer_graph: bool = False,        # PC-algorithm graph discovery
    verbose: bool = True,
)

docs.title: Treatment model override
docs.text:
treatment_model accepts a sub-dict mirroring TabularPipeline, letting the treatment propensity model differ from the outcome model:

treatment_model={"model_name": "TabICLv2", "tuning_strategy": "inference"}

When omitted, the treatment model uses the same TFM as the outcome model.

docs.title: CausalLeaderboard API reference
docs.text:
Rank multiple (estimator × TFM) configurations on the same data.

from tabtune.causal import CausalLeaderboard

lb = CausalLeaderboard(
    treatment="treated",
    outcome="outcome",
    confounders=["age", "income", "score"],
    sensitive=["gender"],
    tuning_params={"device": "cuda"},
)

lb.add_model("TabPFNv26", task_type="regression", estimator="dml")
lb.add_model("TabICLv2",  task_type="regression", estimator="dml")
lb.add_model("TabPFNv26", task_type="regression", estimator="causal_forest",
             estimator_params={"n_estimators": 200})

ranked = lb.run(X_train, y_train, rank_by="refuter_pass_rate")
print(ranked)   # DataFrame: label, model_name, estimator, ate, ci_*, refuter_pass_rate, ...
